en.text: The reusable persona + per-send configuration unit — system prompt, model routing, tools, permissions, twin, voice, and capability gates — resolved into every send by resolveSendOptions, sourced from a Dexie table unioned with plugin character-pack overlays. Characters A Character (角色) is the unit Cognia uses to package who the assistant is and how a send is configured into a single, reusable, selectable object. It is far more than a system prompt: one Character carries the persona prompt, model/provider routing, a tool and MCP subset, a permission mode, skills, an optional Employee Digital Twin binding, a TTS voice overlay, and the on/off gates for computer use, sandbox, OCR, and A2UI. When you pick a Character in the composer, every one of those fields flows into the next turn through exactly one function — resolveSendOptions in lib/claude/build-options.ts. A Character is a row in the Dexie characters table (lib/db/schema.ts:127) unioned at read time with plugin character-pack overlays (ADR-0030) by listCharacters (lib/db/characters.ts:92-120). Overlay rows get synthetic ids cognia-pack: : : ; a Dexie clone with a matching clonedFromPackCharacterId hides its overlay (108-118). The selected Character is resolved by resolveCharacterById (characters.ts:134-141) and collapsed into one SendOptions payload by resolveSendOptions (build-options.ts:369-376). The six default personas now ship as the first-party cognia-builtin-characters plugin pack, seeded into Dexie with attribution by seedBuiltInCharacters (characters.ts:497-560). What a Character Is A Character is per-send configuration with a face . It exists so that all the knobs that shape a turn — prompt, model, tools, permissions, capability gates — can be saved once, named, given an avatar, and re-selected, instead of being re-typed into the composer every time. Selecting a Character binds it to the session (session.characterId); every subsequent send re-resolves it. The Character does not run anything on its own. It is data. The execution spine is the built-in agent: resolveSendOptions reads the Character and folds its fields into the single SendOptions payload that crosses the IPC seam into the sidecar. That convergence is the whole point — a new capability touches the Character schema and one branch of resolveSendOptions, and nothing else. en.text: The standalone .cognia-pack.json file format, the local-pack disk store that sidesteps the marketplace install pipeline, and the selective Apply-Update diff that overwrites pack-managed fields while preserving user edits. Local Packs & Apply Update A character pack can travel as a standalone .cognia-pack.json file imported outside the marketplace install pipeline, and a user's clone of an overlay character can receive a selective update when the pack ships a newer version. This page covers the file format, the disk-backed local-pack store, the per-field diff engine that decides overwrite-vs-preserve, the editor projections, and voice/platform resolution. File format: CHARACTER PACK FILE SCHEMA VERSION = 2, SUPPORTED SCHEMA VERSIONS = Set([1, 2]) — lib/plugin/character-pack/schema.ts:28 / :37. Parser parseLocalPackFile — schema.ts:83-120; serializer serializeLocalPackFile — schema.ts:247-259. Local disk store under local:imported — lib/plugin/character-pack/local-pack-store.ts:51; boot scan scanAndRegisterLocalPacks — :175-222. File format — .cognia-pack.json The file is a thin wrapper carrying a file-format schemaVersion (independent of the pack's semantic version) plus the pack payload and an optional signature. Versioning is two-step: bumping the file format is a host concern; the pack content versions itself via PluginCharacterPackDef.version. Signature verification Signatures are verified, as of 2026-08-03 (ADR-0030 amendment). Unsigned files remain fully supported and are visibly labelled; a signed file whose signature does not verify is refused at import and skipped by the boot scan. The signed bytes are the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of the pack object alone . schemaVersion and signature sit on the wrapper and are stripped before canonicalization — which is exactly why importing a signed v1 file and rewriting it as v2 leaves the signature valid, and why bumping CHARACTER PACK FILE SCHEMA VERSION needs no re-signing campaign. en.title: Chat, Characters, Skills & Teams
en.text: How sessions, messages, characters, skills, teams, and MCP servers compose the chat workspace. Chat, Characters, Skills & Teams The chat workspace is Cognia's largest user-facing surface. Concepts at a glance Concept Owns Persisted in -------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------- Session A conversation thread (title, model, last update) sessions table Message A single user / assistant / tool turn messages table Character A reusable persona (system prompt, model preset, tone, optional twin binding) characters table Skill A reusable capability (prompts, MCP servers, tool allow-list, resources) skills, skillResources tables Team A multi-character routing configuration (delegates between characters) teams table MCP server A tool / resource provider plugged into Claude mcpServers table All persisted in Dexie (IndexedDB); types live in lib/claude/types.ts. Session and message flow The chat store lives in lib/chat/; UI in components/chat/. en.title: Claude Subscription OAuth
en.text: Connect Claude Pro/Max subscription or Console account to the sidecar — OAuth entry, keyring credentials, passive + active usage probes, and real-time visibility into 5h/7d rate limits. Claude Subscription OAuth stable · ADR-0010 Log in to Claude Pro/Max or Console via a paste-back-authorization-code PKCE flow; credentials are kept in the OS keyring, and the sidecar automatically receives Bearer auth through the CLAUDE CODE OAUTH TOKEN environment variable. Every real /v1/messages response is intercepted by fetch-interceptor.mjs, which parses the anthropic-ratelimit-unified- headers and writes them to Dexie, making the 5h / 7d progress bars visible for free. The subscription OAuth subsystem lets Cognia coexist alongside the official claude login CLI without mutual interference: We do not write /.claude/.credentials.json — that file belongs to the Claude Code CLI. We only read the anthropic-ratelimit- response headers — active probes are off by default. The sidecar is strongly bound to the OAuth bearer — when a bearer exists, ANTHROPIC API KEY is explicitly removed, preventing undefined behavior from mixed auth on the SDK side. Code Locations Architecture Overview OAuth Flow Cognia-next uses the paste-back-authorization-code (manual code) variant. We have not registered a loopback redirect, so Anthropic's callback page displays the authorization code directly to the user, who copies it back into the Login dialog. Generate PKCE parameters — buildAuthorizeUrl( mode ) constructs code verifier and derives code challenge from SHA-256 using crypto.randomUUID in the browser, and derives state from the same entropy. Open the authorization URL — the dialog calls tauri-plugin-opener to push the following URL into the system browser: subscription mode: https://claude.ai/oauth/authorize console mode: https://console.anthropic.com/oauth/authorize Both share the client id 9d1c250a-e61b-44d9-88ed-5944d1962f5e (the public value from Claude Code CLI); the server distinguishes modes by host + redirect URI. User pastes the authorization code — extractAuthorizationCode tolerates three paste shapes: full URL, code#state form, and plain code string. Exchange — exchangeCodeForTokens sends an application/x-www-form-urlencoded POST to https://platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token. A JSON body will be rejected by the server with 400 invalid grant — all token requests must be form-encoded

en.text: AcpClientAdapter (acp-client.ts, 2632 lines) — the Agent Client Protocol client. JSON-RPC 2.0 over newline-delimited stdio, the initialize/session.new/prompt-turn flow, the inverted client-side fs & terminal handlers the agent calls back into, the permission bridge, the unstable session/list·fork·resume extensions, and how session/update notifications become the canonical event stream. ACP Client AcpClientAdapter (acp-client.ts:286) speaks the Agent Client Protocol: JSON-RPC 2.0 framed as newline-delimited JSON (split("\n") at :1747). On the desktop it spawns the agent CLI through the Rust bridge (spawn external agent invoke at :397) and listens on external-agent://stdout stderr exit; remote agents use http/ws/sse. The connect handshake sends initialize with protocolVersion: 1 (:714) and advertises the client's fs + terminal capabilities (only under Tauri, :704). ACP inverts the usual client/server roles: once a session is running, the agent calls back into Cognia for fs/read text file, terminal/create, and session/request permission — all dispatched by handleAgentRequest (:1796). Streaming arrives as session/update notifications, which handleSessionUpdate (:2128) turns into the canonical ExternalAgentEvent stream the manager yields. Transport & Framing The adapter extends BaseProtocolAdapter and declares protocol = "acp". connect (:327) branches by transport: stdio (desktop) — connectViaStdio (:377) invokes spawn external agent (:397) with the spawn args from buildSpawnArgs (:271, the exported pure helper that appends --bare/--debug idempotently), then subscribes to external-agent://stdout → handleIncomingMessage (:410). http / websocket / sse — connectViaNetwork (:447) for remote agents, tolerating 404/405 during the connect probe (:462). Incoming bytes are buffered and split on \n in processMessageBuffer (:1739/:1747); each line is JSON-parsed and routed by routeMessage (:1752): an object with a non-null id and a method is an agent→client request (§ Inverted handlers); method with no id is a notification (§ Streaming); a bare id is a response to one of our requests (handleResponse :1777). en.title: External Agents
en.text: The third agent runtime — how Cognia drives external CLI agents (Codex / Claude Code / Gemini / Cursor / OpenCode) as child processes over the Agent Client Protocol and the OpenCode SDK, normalizes them behind one ProtocolAdapter contract, and folds their event streams back into the same chat surface as the built-in agent. External Agents Cognia has three agent runtimes that render into the same chat pane: the built-in agent (in-process Claude Agent SDK), Agent Teams (multi-role squads), and external CLI agents — Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, Cursor, and any OpenCode server — spawned as child processes . The external runtime lives in lib/ai/agent/external/ (14 modules, 15.4k lines). One singleton, ExternalAgentManager (manager.ts:199), runs the whole spine: normalize a raw config (config-normalizer.ts:400) → connect through a protocol adapter picked from a registry (protocol-adapter.ts:474) → open a session → execute a prompt turn (manager.ts:1547 streaming / :1734 headless) → translate the agent's native events into one canonical ExternalAgentEvent stream → project that stream into UIMessage.parts (event-to-parts.ts:53). Every blocking outcome is captured in one canonical contract — ExternalAgentValiditySnapshot — so the UI always knows whether a turn ran externally, fell back to the built-in agent, or was blocked, and why. What It Is An external agent is a third-party coding agent that Cognia does not host in-process. Instead of running the Claude Agent SDK inside the bundled Node sidecar, Cognia spawns the agent's own CLI (or connects to its server) and speaks its wire protocol. Two protocols are implemented: ACP — the Agent Client Protocol, JSON-RPC 2.0 over newline-delimited stdio. This is the path for Codex, Claude Code, Gemini, and Cursor. The client is acp-client.ts (2632 lines). OpenCode — the official @opencode-ai/sdk over HTTP + Server-Sent Events. The client is opencode-client.ts (1659 lines). Both implement one interface, ProtocolAdapter (protocol-adapter.ts:32), so the manager and everything above it (chat, plugins, Agent Teams) never branch on protocol. The architecture exists to satisfy three constraints: 1. The agent is a foreign process. Its filesystem, terminal, and permission model are its own; Cognia is the client . ACP inverts the usual direction — the agent calls back into Cognia for fs/read text file, terminal/create, and session/reques

en.text: Where the external-agent runtime connects to the rest of Cognia — the chat routing chokepoint that picks built-in vs external, the plugin ctx.agent.runExternalAgent API and its agent:dispatch-external permission, the settings UI, the Rust process bridge (spawn external agent + run agent hook), and the localStorage persistence + startup rehydration. Integration Seams The runtime in lib/ai/agent/external/ is self-contained; this page is the map of every place it touches the rest of the app. A chat turn routes to it only when useAgentRuntimeStore.runtime === "external" — checked at use-claude-chat.ts:744, dispatched at :782 via executeOnExternalAgent. Agent Teams drive it through a composite streamer (workspace/page.tsx:137). Plugins reach it through ctx.agent.runExternalAgent (context.ts:662), gated by the agent:dispatch-external permission (:668). Execution itself only happens on the desktop: the Rust external agent module spawns the CLI (commands.rs:34) as a pure stdio pass-through, and run agent hook (hooks/commands.rs:55) runs settings.json hooks. Configs persist to localStorage (key cognia-external-agents), not Dexie, and are rehydrated into the manager at startup. The Integration Map 1 · Chat Routing The runtime is selected by a small store, useAgentRuntimeStore, holding runtime ("claude-sdk" "external") and externalAgentId. The UI picker is components/agent/mode/runtime-selector.tsx (AgentRuntimeSelector) — one radio group holding the built-in claude-sdk runtime plus one row per configured external agent, so picking a lane and picking the agent record are the same click. Rows whose getExternalAgentExecutionBlockReason(...) is non-null render disabled with that reason, and a restored selection that no longer resolves to a runnable agent falls back to claude-sdk instead of parking the composer on an external lane with nothing to dispatch to. A row also carries what the last real contact with the agent found, read from agentValidity[id] (written by useExternalAgent on connect / health check / execution): a failed start shows the runtime's own blockingReason verbatim, a pending sign-in and an unhealthy probe show a translated hint. These are history, not verdicts — a binary missing an hour ago may be installed now — so unlike a config-level block they warn without disabling the row. en.title: Manager (the spine)
en.text: ExternalAgentManager (manager.ts, 2496 lines) — the singleton that owns every external-agent lifecycle. addAgent and connect-with-retry, the executeStreaming interactive chokepoint and the headless execute retry loop, the branch decision, validity & health projection, lifecycle listeners, and rule-based delegation. Manager (the spine) ExternalAgentManager (manager.ts:199) is a process-wide singleton — getExternalAgentManager() (:2460) — that owns the full lifecycle of every external agent. It holds a map of ExternalAgentInstances (:203) and a parallel map of live ProtocolAdapters (:204). addAgent (:966) registers a config, asks the registry for an adapter, and connects; connect (:1072) runs a retry loop with timeout and writes a validitySnapshot on every transition. The two execution methods are the heart: executeStreaming (:1547) is the interactive async-generator that chat and Agent Teams consume — it resolves a session, builds a trace bridge and a hook context, pumps the adapter's event stream, runs the blocking permission gate per event (:1638), and records the outcome; execute (:1734) is the headless, retrying variant. Every status change funnels through updateInstanceState (:830), which normalizes a validitySnapshot so reason codes and branch outcomes are always consistent. Shape & Singleton The manager is a class with a private static instance (:200); getInstance(config?) (:542) lazily constructs and resetInstance() (:552) disposes for tests. The module-level getExternalAgentManager(config?) (:2460) is the canonical accessor used everywhere outside the class. Construction registers the default protocol adapters (registerDefaultAdapters :562) and starts the health-check timer if healthCheckInterval 0 (:217). en.title: OpenCode Adapter
en.text: OpenCodeClientAdapter over the official @opencode-ai/sdk + SSE, plus the ProtocolAdapter contract, the BaseProtocolAdapter.execute event fold, and the registry that selects ACP vs OpenCode without the manager branching on protocol. OpenCode Adapter The second protocol. OpenCodeClientAdapter drives an OpenCode server through the official @opencode-ai/sdk/client — typed HTTP calls plus a Server-Sent Events stream — rather than ACP's JSON-RPC-over-stdio. It connects to http://127.0.0.1:4096 by default (or auto-spawns opencode serve on desktop , or connects to a configured endpoint, optionally with auth). It opens the client.event.subscribe() SSE stream before submitting the prompt with session.promptAsync (so no early streamed parts are missed), then translates each SDK event into the same canonical ExternalAgentEvent stream ACP produces. Both clients extend BaseProtocolAdapter and are looked up by protocol id from protocolAdapterRegistry — so the manager selects ACP vs OpenCode by a single registry.create() call and never branches again. The ProtocolAdapter Contract protocol-adapter.ts is the abstraction that lets two very different wire protocols look identical to the manager. ProtocolAdapterRegistry 474 Factory registry keyed by protocol string; create(protocol) (:499) instantiates the right adapter. The global singleton is protocolAdapterRegistry (:523). SessionCreateOptions (:223) is the shared session-setup payload (cwd, mcpServers, permissionMode, instructionEnvelope :233, systemPrompt, briefMode :248). en.title: Pi Native RPC Adapter
en.text: PiRpcClientAdapter drives pi --mode rpc over Pi's own JSONL command/event protocol, and is now the only way Cognia runs Pi. Covers the strict LF codec and why readline could not be used, the per-session process model, the certified-version policy, the bundled permission extension, the credential diagnostic, and the removal of the community pi-acp bridge. Pi Native RPC Adapter Cognia drives Pi through Pi's own protocol , not ACP. pi --mode rpc speaks a JSONL command/event stream where frames are bare type, id objects answered by "type":"response", command, success, data — close enough to JSON-RPC to be mistaken for it, and different enough that reusing the JSON-RPC peer would mis-route every event. The adapter keeps thinking levels, the steering and follow-up queues, the compaction lifecycle, session forks and usage detail that the community pi-acp bridge flattened away (that bridge has since been removed entirely). See ADR-0119. Why not readline Every other external agent's stdout is framed by the shared host with readline. Pi cannot use it. Node's readline treats U+2028 and U+2029 as line terminators, and JSON.stringify does not escape them. A single valid Pi frame whose payload contains U+2028 — which appears in real text copied from the web and in model output — arrives split into several unparseable fragments. So pi-rpc opts into a raw-chunk forwarding mode (framing: "raw" on the spawn config, delivered base64 on external-agent://stdout-raw) and frames the bytes itself in pi-rpc-peer.ts: split on the 0x0A byte only; strip one trailing \r so CRLF still parses a lone \r is not a delimiter — inside JSON a carriage return must be escaped, so treating one as a boundary could only ever break a well-formed frame decode per frame, not per chunk, so a chunk boundary inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence cannot produce replacement characters 16 MiB per frame and 32 MiB of unterminated buffer, past which the session ends with protocol frame invalid The Rust host is byte-oriented and was already correct; only the Node host needed the new path. ACP, Codex and OpenCode keep the existing readline path unchanged. Correlation Three behaviours were established by running Pi 0.84.1, and each defeats an obvious implementation: Observed Consequence --- --- Responses are not FIFO — an abort reply landed after a later get state Correlate by id only; ordering means nothing A malfo

en.title: Event Translation
en.text: How a foreign agent's output becomes Cognia's chat — translators.ts (981 lines) converts between the internal agent/tool model and ACP (including a full JSON-Schema→Zod tool bridge and the events→steps fold), and event-to-parts.ts (208 lines) is the pure mapper that projects a canonical ExternalAgentEvent stream into UIMessage.parts the renderer already understands. Event Translation Two pure modules sit between the protocol clients and the chat renderer. translators.ts does the model translation: ACP tool definitions → executable AgentTools via a full JSON-Schema→Zod compiler (acpToolToAgentTool :82, jsonSchemaToZod :163), Cognia ToolCall ⇄ ACP tool-use, ExternalAgentResult ⇄ SubAgentResult (so external agents can act as Agent-Team members), and a set of stream folds that reduce an ExternalAgentEvent[] into response text, thinking, tool calls, and ExternalAgentStep[] (eventsToSteps :721). event-to-parts.ts does the render translation: a stateless reducer (applyExternalAgentEventToParts :53) that applies one event to the current parts[] and returns the next — message delta → text/reasoning parts, tool use start → a tool- part (or an artifact part), tool result → output/error on that part. The renderer then treats an external turn exactly like a built-in one. (+ artifact)" / translators.ts — Model Translation The file is organized into banner-delimited concern groups: message translators (:25), tool translators (:72), result translators (:547), event translators (:637), permission translators (:829), and content helpers (:859). en.title: Type & Contract
en.text: types/agent/external-agent.ts (2168 lines) — the single source of truth for the external-agent runtime. The protocol/transport taxonomy, the full ACP type surface, the config/session/message/event models, the canonical validity & branch-reason types, and the serialization helpers and type guards every other module depends on. Type & Contract types/agent/external-agent.ts is the contract the whole runtime is typed against — 2168 lines, zero runtime logic beyond serialization helpers and type guards. It declares six type families: the protocol/transport taxonomy (ExternalAgentProtocol, :16), the canonical diagnostics model (ExternalAgentBranchReasonCode :36, ExternalAgentBranchOutcome :59, ExternalAgentValiditySnapshot :255), the ACP wire types (Acp , :325–:1032), the configuration model (ExternalAgentConfig :1122), the session/message model (ExternalAgentSession :1233), and the streaming event union (ExternalAgentEvent :1673, 21 variants). Everything downstream — manager, clients, translators, UI — imports from here and nowhere else for these shapes. The Protocol/Transport Taxonomy Two orthogonal axes describe how Cognia reaches an agent. They are declared first because every other type keys off them. en.title: /goal command
en.text: Set a standing goal and the agent auto-continues until done, paused, or out of budget. /goal — Persistent Chat Goals cognia-next's /goal command turns any chat into a self-driving loop. You set the objective in one line, the agent picks the next concrete step, completes it, evaluates whether the objective is satisfied, and continues automatically until (a) a judge model says it's done, (b) the turn / token / time budget is exhausted, or (c) you pause or stop it. Inspired by the /goal commands in Hermes Agent , OpenAI Codex CLI , and Anthropic Claude Code — and fused into one design that takes the best of each. Architecture details: see ADR-0019. Quick start A pill appears just above the composer: The agent posts its first response. When the response stops streaming, cognia-next: 1. Records the turn against the goal (turnsUsed += 1, tokensUsed += ). 2. Calls a judge LLM with the goal + the response → "done": true false, "reason": "..." . 3. If done, the goal moves to completed. The agent stops. 4. If not, the next turn fires automatically. No Enter needed. All seven subcommands Command Aliases Behaviour --------------------- ---------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- /goal /goal create Create a new goal. If one is already open, it's terminated first. /goal status (also: empty /goal) Print a status card with progress + last judge reason. /goal show Same as status, plus opens the Goals settings tab. /goal pause Pause the loop without losing state. Resumable. /goal resume Resume a paused goal. The next continuation fires immediately. /goal stop /goal cancel /goal clear Terminate the goal as stopped. /goal update Replace the objective in place. Bumps generationId so any in-flight judge is dropped. All subcommands refuse while a turn is still streaming — they wait for the SDK to settle before mutating the goal row. Exit conditions (seven layers, in priority order) # Trigger Resulting status --- ------------------------------------------------------ --------------------------- 1 /goal stop (or cancel / clear) stopped (terminal) 2 User typed a fresh non-slash message mid-loop preempted (terminal) 3 turnsUsed = maxTurns (default 20) turn limited (terminal) 4 tokensUsed = maxTokens (default 200k) budget limited (terminal) 5 Date.now() - createdAt = timeoutMs (default 30 min) timed out (terminal) 6

en.title: Provider System
en.text: A directory of 70+ built-in providers, API key persistence, dynamic registry, local inference service discovery, and a projection layer that folds all paths into a unified selector. Provider System stable Cognia maintains 70+ built-in providers (OpenAI / Anthropic / Google / DeepSeek / local Ollama …) in a static catalog, maps them to 5 adapters across 6 protocol families; plugins can dynamically register their own providers; finally, a pure-function projection layer merges built-in + custom + local + plugin paths into a flat array for the UI. The Provider System covers five responsibilities: 1. Catalog — metadata for 70+ built-in providers (id, display name, protocol, pricing, model list). 2. Adapter — maps providers to 5 unified HTTP clients. 3. Registry — dynamically registered providers at plugin runtime. 4. Persistence — API keys (OS keyring) + user preferences (Dexie settings) + verification state. 5. Projection — folds all sources into a unified projection for the UI / picker. The OAuth subscription path has its own subsystem; see Claude Subscription OAuth. Embedding-only providers are consumed through Vector Store. en.title: Slash Commands
en.text: A unified slash-command registry spanning three sources (built-in / custom / plugin), composer triggering, template insertion, and Action dispatch. Slash Commands Slash commands (/ [args]) are "quick shortcuts" inside chat. Cognia unifies three sources — built-in Actions, local .md templates, and plugin contributions — into a single registry. The composer pops a picker when the user types /, and dispatches along one of two paths: Action or Template. The picker ranks candidates with the shared fuzzy matcher (lib/chat/completion/fuzzy-match.ts) — the same scorer the @-mention picker uses — matching the command name first and its description as a demoted secondary source, so /gc surfaces git/commit and the closest match sorts to the top. Single registry (lib/slash-commands/registry.ts) + built-in commands (builtin.ts) + custom markdown (custom.ts, scans .claude/commands/ .md) + plugin contributions. Composer shows picker → Action executes immediately (SlashContext), Template inserts into the text box and supports $1..$9 / $ARGUMENTS placeholder substitution. Rust side slash commands scan parses frontmatter and recursively scans directories. Use Cases Add a "quick action" for Cognia (clear session / switch model / open MCP panel …). Reuse a prompt template ("code-review the changes …") so the user types /review to drop the template into the input box for further editing. Let plugins register discoverable commands (e.g. git-tools.status) and surface them in the Settings UI with one-click discovery. Stay compatible with external Claude Code's existing /.claude/commands/ .md / /.claude/commands/ .md. en.title: Cloudflare Tunnel (persistent WAN access)
en.text: Expose Cognia's companion server over a stable public hostname with a named Cloudflare Tunnel, so mobile clients reconnect across restarts. A hands-on guide you run manually before the in-app flow lands. Cloudflare Tunnel (persistent WAN access) Cognia's companion server lets your phone reach your home desktop. On the same Wi-Fi that happens over the LAN; off-network it needs a path through the internet. Cognia already ships a one-click Quick Tunnel , but a Quick Tunnel hands you a random .trycloudflare.com URL that changes every time it restarts — so the baseUrl your phone stored at pairing time goes stale and the phone can no longer connect. This guide sets up a named Cloudflare Tunnel bound to a hostname on a domain you own. The URL is stable across restarts , so a phone paired once keeps reconnecting — no re-pairing. This is the manual procedure. You run cloudflared yourself and configure the hostname in the Cloudflare dashboard. It is also the validation path for the upcoming in-app Named tunnel config (paste a token + hostname, one-click run) — the moving parts are identical, so what you verify here is exactly what the app will automate. Quick Tunnel vs named tunnel Quick Tunnel (built-in today) Named tunnel (this guide) --- --- --- Cloudflare account / domain Not needed Required (domain on Cloudflare DNS) Public URL Random, changes on restart Fixed hostname you pick Limits 200 concurrent requests, no SSE, no SLA Standard Cloudflare proxy limits Good for Quick test, throwaway link Daily/long-term phone access Prerequisites A Cloudflare account with a domain already on Cloudflare DNS (the domain's nameservers point at Cloudflare). If you don't have one, add a site in the Cloudflare dashboard first — a named tunnel cannot attach a hostname to a domain Cloudflare doesn't manage. cloudflared installed on the desktop running Cognia: Or download the binary from Cloudflare downloads. Install via APT/RPM or download the binary — see Cloudflare downloads. Verify: Steps ### Start Cognia's companion server In Cognia (desktop): Settings → Companion → Server . Start the server and note the port — the default is 27890 . The loopback bind mode is fine here: cloudflared runs on the same machine and connects to localhost, so you do not need LAN mode. Cognia serves HTTPS with a self-signed certificate . Confirm it's up locally by opening https://localhost:27890 in a bro

en.title: Public share links (zero-knowledge)
en.text: Self-host the Cognia share worker on Cloudflare (R2 + KV) so you can turn a chat export, workflow image, A2UI app, or backup into a short public link. Contents are end-to-end encrypted in your browser; the server only ever stores ciphertext. Public share links (zero-knowledge) Cognia can turn an artifact — a chat transcript, a workflow diagram, an A2UI app, or a backup package — into a short URL anyone can open in a browser. The content is end-to-end encrypted on your device : a random key is generated locally, placed in the URL #fragment, and never uploaded . The worker stores only opaque ciphertext, and decryption happens in the recipient's browser. The #fragment is never sent to any server, so the host cannot read your shares even in principle. This is a self-hosted, single-tenant model, mirroring the signaling server: you deploy the worker to your own Cloudflare account and point the app at it. Reads are public (anyone with the link); creating and revoking links requires a bearer secret only you hold. Free-tier friendly: Cloudflare R2 (10 GB free), Workers KV, and Workers all have free tiers sufficient for personal use. What gets shared Artifact Viewer renders it as --- --- Chat export (HTML / animated) Inline, in a sandboxed iframe Chat export (Markdown / JSON / text) Preformatted text Workflow image A PNG Backup package A download (re-import under Settings → Data) A2UI app Rendered live in the browser (read-only) Prerequisites A Cloudflare account, and wrangler installed (npm i -g wrangler, then wrangler login). Optional: a domain on Cloudflare DNS if you want a custom hostname (share.example.com); otherwise the worker is reachable on .workers.dev. Deploy the worker (the API) The worker lives in services/share-server/worker/. It is a standalone project (not part of the app's pnpm workspace) and is now a pure JSON API — the viewer is the app's own /share/view route, deployed separately to Cloudflare Pages (next section). wrangler.toml scopes the Worker to share.cognia.cn/v1/ so Cloudflare Pages can serve the viewer on the same host — change the hostname to your own (requires that zone active on your account), or comment the routes line out to use the .workers.dev subdomain only. Deploy the viewer (Cloudflare Pages) The viewer is the app's /share/view route, shipped in the normal static export. Build the app and deploy out/ to Pages on the same host

en.title: BYO TURN credentials
en.text: How to plug a TURN server into the WebRTC tier when ICE direct connection fails. ADR-0021 deliberately ships without bundled TURN — users bring their own. BYO TURN credentials Cognia's WebRTC tier (ADR-0021) tries to open a direct DataChannel between the mobile app and the home desktop. On the common NAT topologies (full-cone, restricted-cone, port-restricted) STUN-based hole punching is enough. On symmetric NAT — most commonly seen on cellular carriers and hotel guest networks — STUN can't get through and the tier falls back to cloudflared or LAN. If you regularly hit symmetric NAT (cellular while travelling, certain office VPNs, university Wi-Fi), plugging a TURN server gets you a WebRTC-relayed path that still avoids the cloudflared tunnel. What you need A TURN server with username + credential. Cognia does not bundle one; pick a provider. Three good options below. Settings → Mobile companion → WebRTC card → "TURN servers" textarea. One line per server, format turn:host:port?transport=udp user cred. Twilio Network Traversal Service (paid, pay-as-you-go) 1. Create a Twilio account and get an Account SID + Auth Token. 2. Generate ephemeral credentials via the Twilio REST API: 3. The response contains username, password, and a list of ice servers. Paste the TURN URLs (transport=udp first) into the "TURN servers" textarea: 4. Twilio credentials are time-limited (default 24h). The Cognia UI does not refresh them automatically — re-paste when they expire, or move to a self-hosted server below. Cloudflare Calls TURN (free tier available) 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, navigate to Calls → TURN servers. 2. Create a TURN application; copy the issued key ID + API token. 3. Use curl (or the Cloudflare SDK) to mint credentials at start of each session — the workflow is identical in shape to Twilio: 4. Paste the returned URLs into the "TURN servers" textarea, same format as Twilio. Self-hosted coturn (free, requires a VPS) 1. On a public-IP VPS (Hetzner / DigitalOcean / Linode), install coturn: 2. Edit /etc/turnserver.conf: 3. Open UDP/TCP 3478 (and 5349 for TLS) in your VPS firewall. If your VPS uses cloud-managed firewalls, allow the relay-port range too (default 49152–65535) or restrict via min-port / max-port in turnserver.conf. 4. sudo systemctl enable --now coturn. 5. Paste into the Cognia "TURN servers" textarea: Verifying it works After saving, in the desktop

en.title: WebRTC verification checklist
en.text: Real-device smoke test for the WebRTC mobile↔desktop tier (ADR-0021). Run after every change that touches the SDP/ICE handshake, the signaling envelope schema, or the pair flow. WebRTC verification checklist Use this checklist after any change that could affect the WebRTC tier end-to-end: signaling envelope schema, SDP/ICE handshake, pair-flow mints, rendezvous-server upgrades, or the TransportRtc state machine. The automated pnpm webrtc:smoke covers the rendezvous-server side only — this checklist exercises both mobile (Capacitor) ↔ desktop (Tauri) and browser (Web Companion) ↔ desktop/cloud paths. Setup You need: A desktop machine with the latest pnpm tauri dev build. A phone with the matching mobile build (pnpm mobile:sync + Xcode / Android Studio). A production Web build served from an allowed HTTPS origin. Unlock its browser Vault and pair it to the same host with the invite link or payload. The phone on cellular (not the same Wi-Fi as the desktop) — that forces the WebRTC tier to do real NAT traversal rather than landing on ws-lan. A scratch room for diagnostics: open chrome://webrtc-internals on the desktop, and the Cognia app's Settings → Mobile companion → WebRTC card on both sides. Step 1 — Pair and observe tier rollup 1. From the desktop, generate a pair QR (Settings → Mobile companion → Pair device → Generate QR). 2. On the phone, run the in-app pair flow: Discover → Pair → scan the cgnp3 QR. The phone completes challenge + P-256 registration at POST /api/auth/device/register; this returns a RoomDescriptor and stores the independent mobile-role signaling key in secure storage. 3. Within 5 seconds the desktop's WebRTC card should show the new device transitioning offline → awaiting → negotiating → connected . 4. On the mobile Settings panel, the Transport row should land on WebRTC (direct). The "Reconnect WebRTC" button is visible. If the tier stays on ws-tunnel (i.e. cloudflared) or offline after a minute, jump to Step 4. Step 2 — Selected ICE candidate type 1. With the DataChannel open, open chrome://webrtc-internals on the desktop. 2. Find the RTCDataChannel:cognia.signaling row → expand the parent peer connection → RTCIceCandidatePair → look at the local candidate's type. 3. Expected: host (same LAN; you shouldn't be on cellular if so) or srflx (typical cellular). prflx is also fine. If the type is relay, see Step 4. 4. Screenshot this row for

Create an enterprise internal app and enable the robot capability for that app. 3. Record these credentials from the app credential page: App Key - used as the Stream Mode clientId. App Secret - used as the Stream Mode clientSecret and to mint app access tokens. Keep the App Secret private. cognia-next stores both values in the OS keyring. --- 2. Release or publish the updated app version if the console requires it. cognia-next registers the Stream connection by calling: The runtime then opens the returned WebSocket endpoint with the one-time ticket and ACKs each callback frame. en.title: Extending Platform Connectors with Plugins
en.text: How to write a cognia-next plugin that contributes a new messaging-platform adapter. Extending Platform Connectors with Plugins cognia-next ships eleven built-in platform adapters: Telegram, Discord, Slack, Lark, OneBot, DingTalk, WeCom (企业微信), WeChat Official Account, personal WeChat, QQ Official, and Matrix. The Plugin Connector Bridge (lib/plugin/bridge/connectors-bridge.ts) lets any installed plugin contribute additional adapters — Mastodon, Bluesky, or an internal messaging system — without touching the cognia-next source. Email, KOOK, LINE, and Mattermost remain explicitly planned and are not counted as available adapters. How it works 1. The plugin declares "connectors" in capabilities and a connectors[] array in its manifest. 2. On plugin enable, registerPluginAdapters() calls the factory function from the plugin's exported module and hands the resulting PlatformAdapter to the ConnectorBus. 3. The adapter then participates in the full pipeline: inbound dedup → policy evaluation → mode routing → outbound FIFO queue → circuit breaker → audit log. Walkthrough — hypothetical Mastodon adapter 1. Declare the capability in manifest.json 2. Export the factory function 3. Register / unregister via the bridge The bridge is called automatically by the plugin lifecycle when the user enables or disables the plugin. You do not need to call it manually — the PluginManager handles this. For debugging you can call the bridge directly: Accessing credentials Use the Tauri keyring shims to store and retrieve secrets: Credentials are stored encrypted in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, libsecret on Linux). They are never logged or included in backups. Transport patterns Pattern When to use ------------ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ longpoll REST-based platforms with a "get updates" endpoint (Telegram, Mastodon). webhook Platform pushes to a public URL via axum. reverse-ws Device connects to cognia-next (OneBot / NapCat pattern). gateway Maintain a long-lived WS to the platform (Discord). For webhook and reverse-ws you need to register an axum route in the Rust connector module. See src-tauri/src/connectors/ for examples. Coverage requirement Plugin-contributed adapters are subject to the same ≥90% test coverage rule as built-in code (see CLAUDE.md). Ship tests alongside your plugin using the same foo.t

en.title: Local Live Testing
en.text: Drive a real Telegram, Slack, Discord, Lark or Matrix conversation against your configured Cognia bot, with the model swapped for a deterministic fixture. Local Live Testing Every other connector test in this repo fakes at least one end. The mocked E2E suites fake the platform; scripts/lark-live-smoke.mts hits the real Feishu API but only outbound, through a Node stand-in for Tauri. Neither proves the thing you actually care about: that a real message, pushed by a real platform, through the real transport (Feishu's long connection and every webhook signature live in Rust), past the real admission gates and the PII gate, comes back as a real reply. This harness closes that loop. The only substitution is the model: a deterministic fixture stands in for Anthropic so assertions are stable and the runs cost nothing. What you need Two identities per platform — a driver that posts, and the target bot you already run in Cognia — plus a dedicated conversation only these two are in. The driver never reuses Cognia's own adapter code; it talks to the platform's API directly, so one bug cannot cancel itself out on both sides. The target bot must already be configured, enabled, and set to auto-reply in that conversation. This harness never writes your database, keyring, or connector configuration. Commands Terminal 1. Starts a loopback-only model fixture, then launches pnpm tauri dev with ANTHROPIC BASE URL pointed at it. Leave it running. It publishes test-results/im-live/target.json (mode 0600) so the runner can find the fixture and authenticate to its control plane. Terminal 2. Preflight only — posts nothing. Checks the driver's identity really differs from the target's, the credential has the right shape, the conversation is reachable, and the fixture is up. The P0 scenario. Use --platform all for every platform (it refuses to start unless all five are configured; add --allow-unconfigured to run what you have and report the rest as NOT CONFIGURED). Two more commands need no credentials and no running app: im:test:unit covers the harness itself. im:test:contract aggregates the existing connector transport, contract, dedup and rate-limit suites. Note one gap it does not close: slack/transport-socket-mode.test.ts has no disconnect/reconnect case, where Discord and Matrix both do — a green contract run is not proof of full protocol coverage. Register a dedicated bot account on that homeserver, for example @bot:matrix.org. Use a separate account rather than your personal one. 3. OneBot (QQ) Setup Guide cognia-next connects to QQ through the OneBot protocol over two WebSocket topologies: Reverse WS : NapCat, Lagrange, or LLOneBot runs alongside the QQ client and dials into the cognia-next connector server. en.title: QQ Official Bot Setup
en.text: Create a QQ Official Bot, get the App ID and Client Secret, and connect through the WebSocket gateway. QQ Official Bot Setup Guide This guide walks through creating an officially authorized bot in the QQ Open Platform , collecting the App ID and Client Secret , and connecting cognia-next through the QQ WebSocket gateway. This is the official QQ bot channel and is separate from the unofficial OneBot / NapCat path. --- 1. Create a Bot in the QQ Open Platform 1. Open https://q.qq.com and sign in to the QQ Open Platform. 2. Create a bot application, then open Bot → Development Settings . 3. Record these credentials: App ID — the bot application identifier, usually shaped like 102xxxxxx. AppSecret — the application secret; cognia-next calls this Client Secret . 4. Complete the platform-side setup you need: Configure event subscription intents . cognia-next subscribes to channel messages, group / C2C messages, and direct-message events. Test in the sandbox environment first. Submit the bot for production review before expecting it to receive and send messages in the live environment. --- 2. Configure the Adapter in cognia-next 1. Open cognia-next and navigate to Settings → Platform Connections → Adapters . 2. Click Add connector , then choose QQ Official Bot . 3. Fill in: Display name — a recognizable name for this bot, for example "My QQ Bot". App ID — the application identifier from Bot → Development Settings . Client Secret — the QQ Open Platform AppSecret . cognia-next uses it to mint access tokens. 4. Click Create . The App ID and Client Secret are encrypted in the OS keyring. The adapter uses them to call https://bots.qq.com/app/getAppAccessToken, caches the short-lived access token, resolves the gateway URL through GET /gateway, and then connects over WebSocket. Like Discord Gateway mode, this is a persistent outbound connection and does not require a public webhook URL. --- 3. Verify the Connection 1. Mention the bot in a channel, or send it a direct / group message if those abilities are enabled for your bot. 2. The message should appear in cognia-next within a few seconds. 3. Check Platform Connections — the adapter status should show running . If the adapter shows stopped or degraded : Confirm the App ID and Client Secret are correct. Confirm the bot has passed QQ Open Platform production review and the required event intents are enabled. Open Settings

en.title: QQ via OneBot — FAQ
en.text: Common questions about the OneBot QQ integration: UIN vs OpenID, multi-account setups, NapCat vs Lagrange, and known limitations. QQ via OneBot — FAQ Why UIN instead of OpenID? cognia-next's OneBot adapter uses the bot's UIN (QQ number), which is what NapCat, Lagrange, and LLOneBot expose. The QQ Official Bot platform uses OpenID — a completely different API with the official Bot gateway and REST endpoints. Use the separate qq-official adapter for that path. Do not mix the two: NapCat does not understand OpenID, and the QQ Official Bot API does not use OneBot. --- Group permission requirements For the bot to receive group messages the bot account must be: A member of the group. (For @-mention responses) the group must allow any member to be @-mentioned, OR the bot must be explicitly mentioned. Some groups restrict messaging to admins. In that case only admins can trigger the bot; cognia-next respects the OneBot event stream as-is. --- Reverse-WS firewall / connection refused By default cognia-next's connectors server binds to 127.0.0.1 (loopback only). This means: NapCat and cognia-next must run on the same machine . If you run NapCat on a different host (e.g. a Docker container on the same LAN), the connection will fail. Solutions: 1. Run NapCat on the same host as cognia-next. 2. If separation is required, use ssh -L 7842:127.0.0.1:7842 user@cognia-host to forward the default connectors port. 3. A future setting will allow binding to 0.0.0.0 — watch the changelog. --- Token rotation If you change the bearer token in NapCat or cognia-next: 1. Update the token in cognia-next Settings → Connections → (adapter) → Bearer Token . 2. Update the accessToken in NapCat config. 3. Restart or reconnect NapCat so it opens a new WebSocket with the new token. You do not need to restart cognia-next. The reverse-WS server reads the keyring on each WebSocket upgrade, so the saved token is used by the next connection. For forward WS, cognia-next sends the saved token as Authorization: Bearer when it dials the OneBot client's WebSocket server. --- Frame size limits OneBot clients typically cap individual WS frames at a few MB. If you send a very large file, the upload will fail with a frame-size error from NapCat. Use the file segment type for large attachments: NapCat will upload the file via the QQ file transfer API and send a reference rather than embedding raw bytes. ---

en.title: Slack Bot Setup
en.text: Create a Slack app, gather bot/app tokens and signing secret, and connect it to cognia-next. Slack Bot Setup Guide This guide walks you through creating a Slack app, obtaining the required tokens and secrets, and configuring cognia-next to connect to your workspace. --- 1. Create a Slack App 1. Open https://api.slack.com/apps and sign in with your Slack account. 2. Click Create New App and choose From scratch . 3. Enter an App Name (e.g. "Cognia Bot") and select the workspace you want to install it in. 4. Click Create App . --- 2. Add OAuth Scopes 1. In your app settings, select OAuth & Permissions from the left sidebar. 2. Scroll down to Bot Token Scopes and add the following: Scope Purpose ------------------- ----------------------------------------- chat:write Send messages to channels and DMs channels:history Read messages in public channels im:history Read messages in direct messages (DMs) app mentions:read Receive events when the bot is @mentioned users:read Look up user information users:read.email (Optional) Access user email addresses 3. Click Save Changes . --- 3. Choose the inbound transport cognia-next supports two Slack inbound transports: Socket Mode (default): cognia-next dials Slack over a persistent WebSocket. No public URL is required. This mode needs an app-level xapp-... token. Events API webhook : Slack calls cognia-next through a public HTTPS Request URL. This mode needs the Signing Secret and a running public tunnel. For the default Socket Mode path: 1. In your app settings, select Socket Mode from the left sidebar. 2. Toggle Enable Socket Mode to on. 3. You will be prompted to Generate an App-Level Token : Enter a token name (e.g. "cognia-socket-token"). Add the scope connections:write. Click Generate . 4. Copy the token — it starts with xapp-. Store it securely. For the Events API webhook path: 1. In cognia-next, create the Slack adapter with Events API webhook selected, then reopen it after saving. 2. Start the Cloudflared tunnel in Settings → Companion → Tunnel . 3. Copy the generated Request URL from the Slack configuration dialog. 4. In Slack, open Event Subscriptions , enable events, and paste that URL as the Request URL . --- 4. Install the App to Your Workspace 1. In your app settings, select OAuth & Permissions from the left sidebar. 2. Click Install to Workspace (or Reinstall if already installed). 3. Review the permissions

en.title: Telegram Bot Setup
en.text: Create a bot with @BotFather, get the Bot Token, and connect it to cognia-next through long polling or webhook delivery. Telegram Bot Setup Guide This guide walks through creating a Telegram bot with @BotFather, collecting its Bot Token, and connecting it to cognia-next through either long polling or webhook delivery. --- 1. Create a Bot with @BotFather 1. Open @BotFather in Telegram and start a chat. 2. Send /newbot, then follow the prompts: Name — the display name shown in chats, for example "Cognia Bot". Username — globally unique and ending in bot, for example cognia workspace bot. 3. After creation, @BotFather returns a Bot Token shaped like 1234567890:ABCDEF.... Store it securely; anyone with this token can control the bot. Optional @BotFather settings: Command Purpose --- --- /setprivacy Group privacy mode. When enabled, the bot only receives messages that mention it or reply to it. When disabled, it can receive all group messages. /setcommands Registers slash commands so users see command hints in the Telegram composer. If you want the bot to passively receive all group messages, disable privacy mode with /setprivacy and re-add the bot to the group if needed. --- 2. Configure cognia-next 1. Open cognia-next and navigate to Settings → Platform Connections . 2. Open the Adapters tab, click Add connector , then choose Telegram . 3. In the Telegram configuration dialog, fill in: Field Description --- --- Display name Internal name for this bot, for example "My Workspace Bot". Bot Token The token from @BotFather. It is encrypted in the OS keyring and never written to logs. Transport Long polling (default): cognia-next polls Telegram and needs no public URL. Webhook : Telegram pushes updates to your public URL. 4. In the desktop app, click Test after entering the token. It calls Telegram getMe and shows the bot username and id on success. The Test button requires the Tauri desktop runtime. It is disabled in browser-only mode. 5. Click Create . --- 3. Configure Public Ingress (Webhook Only) If you selected Webhook , Telegram needs a public HTTPS endpoint, and cognia-next needs to be able to tell Telegram about it. 1. Open Settings → Platform Connections → Tunnel and start the Cloudflared Tunnel there. Start it from the Tunnel tab, not from Mobile Companion . en.title: WeChat Official Account Setup
en.text: Configure WeChat Official Account server safe mode, connect the callback webhook to cognia-next, and store the credentials used for signature verification and AES-256-CBC decryption. WeChat Official Account Setup Guide This guide walks through enabling server configuration in the WeChat Official Account platform, connecting its webhook to cognia-next, and storing the access-token and safe-mode decryption credentials. SHA-1 signature verification and AES-256-CBC body decryption are handled by the Rust webhook handler in cognia-next. --- 1. Prepare an Official Account 1. Prepare a WeChat Official Account. A Service Account is recommended because Subscription Accounts have restricted developer APIs and may not support the customer-service reply API you need. 2. Sign in to WeChat Official Accounts Platform, then open Settings and Development → Basic Configuration . 3. Record the AppID and AppSecret . The full AppSecret is shown only when generated or reset, so store it securely. --- 2. Configure Credentials in cognia-next 1. Open cognia-next and navigate to Settings → Platform Connections → Adapters . 2. Click Add connector , then choose WeChat Official Account . 3. In the Identity section, fill in all four fields: Field Purpose --- --- App ID The AppID from Basic Configuration App Secret The AppSecret , used to mint access token and call the customer-service reply API Token The exact token you will configure in WeChat server settings for signature verification EncodingAESKey The 43-character safe-mode key used to decrypt callback bodies 4. Click Create . All four values are encrypted in the OS keyring and are not stored in plaintext settings. 5. Reopen the saved adapter. The Delivery section now shows the real webhook URL because the adapter id exists. --- 3. Configure the WeChat Server Callback 1. In the saved adapter's Delivery section, copy the Webhook URL . When the Cloudflared Tunnel is running, it should be a full public HTTPS URL shaped like https://.../webhook/wechat-oa/ adapterId . If only /webhook/wechat-oa/ adapterId is shown, prepend your public HTTPS base URL manually or start the tunnel first. 2. In the WeChat Official Accounts Platform, open Settings and Development → Basic Configuration → Server Configuration , click Modify configuration , and enter: URL : the full public HTTPS webhook URL. Token : exactly the same value you saved in cognia-next

en.title: Personal WeChat (iLink) Setup
en.text: Connect a personal WeChat account through the iLink gateway with QR login. Unofficial, reply-only, and carries account-ban risk. Personal WeChat (iLink) Setup Guide This guide walks you through connecting a personal WeChat account to cognia-next through the iLink gateway . --- 1. Read the Risk Notice Review these constraints before you start: This connector uses the iLink gateway (https://ilinkai.weixin.qq.com). It is an unofficial integration path, not an official WeChat bot capability. Automating a personal WeChat account may violate WeChat's terms and carries a real account-ban risk . Use a non-primary WeChat account. Do not connect an account that has payments, critical contacts, or work communication attached to it. Because the path is unofficial and gateway-dependent, availability, protocol shape, and limits can change without notice. Use an official connector such as WeCom or Slack when you cannot accept those risks. --- 2. Sign In With QR Login iLink does not have static credentials. Login is completed by scanning a QR code with the WeChat mobile app. QR login depends on the gateway and is available only in the desktop runtime (Tauri). 1. Open cognia-next and go to Settings → Connections → Adapters . 2. Click Add adapter and choose Personal WeChat (iLink) . 3. Enter a Display name for the connector, for example WeChat side account. 4. Click Get login QR . The dialog shows a QR image. 5. Scan it with WeChat on your phone and confirm the login on the phone. 6. The dialog status advances automatically: waiting for scan → scanned → confirmed . 7. After confirmation, the gateway returns bot token and baseurl. cognia-next persists bot token in the OS keyring as botToken, and stores baseurl in the adapter settings. 8. Click Create to finish. If the QR code expires, click Get login QR again to generate a new one. --- 3. Verify the Connection This channel is reply-only , so verification must start from the WeChat side: 1. Ask any WeChat contact to send a message to the connected account. 2. Once cognia-next receives that message, it can reply in the same WeChat conversation. 3. Check Settings → Connections . The adapter should show as running . If the adapter shows degraded or stopped : session expired rescan means the gateway session expired. Reopen the adapter dialog and scan a fresh QR code. Check the Audit Log tab under Connections for the exact platform

en.title: WeCom AI Bot Setup
en.text: Connect a WeCom AI Bot with BotID and long-connection Secret, including streaming replies, welcome cards, and quick-command menu cards. WeCom AI Bot Setup Guide This guide walks through creating a WeCom AI Bot , collecting the long-connection credentials, and configuring cognia-next to connect through WeCom's long-lived WebSocket channel. The long connection is maintained by the desktop connector runtime, so it does not require a public URL, encrypted callback mode, or an IP allowlist. --- 1. Create a WeCom AI Bot 1. Sign in to the WeCom admin console. 2. Open App Management and create an AI Bot . 3. Record these credentials from the bot detail page: BotID — the AI Bot identifier, usually shaped like wb1234567890abcdef. Long-connection Secret — the secret dedicated to the AI Bot long connection. Important: the long-connection Secret is not the same as callback-mode Token / EncodingAESKey. The AI Bot long connection does not use callback mode, does not need a public URL, does not encrypt callback payloads, and does not require an IP allowlist. --- 2. Configure cognia-next 1. Open cognia-next and navigate to Settings → Platform Connections → Adapters . 2. Click Add connector , then choose WeCom AI Bot . 3. In the Identity section, fill in: Display name — a recognizable name for this bot. Bot ID — the wb... BotID from the WeCom admin console. Secret — the long-connection Secret from the bot detail page. Welcome message (optional) — text to send when WeCom emits an enter chat event. Leave it blank to skip welcome text. 4. Click Create . The Bot ID and Secret are encrypted in the OS keyring. Non-secret settings such as the welcome message are stored in adapter settings. After the adapter is enabled, it performs the aibot subscribe handshake, sends a ping every 30 seconds, and reconnects with exponential backoff after disconnects. --- 3. Configure Quick Commands (Optional) WeCom AI Bot does not have a persistent native menu. cognia-next approximates one by sending a template card menu card on enter chat: 1. In the dialog, open the Quick commands section. 2. Add command rows. Each row becomes a menu-card button bound to either a prompt or a slash command . 3. When a user clicks a menu button, cognia-next routes the mapped prompt or slash command as a user message into the runtime. The menu card displays up to six buttons. en.title: Architecture
en.text: A layered view of Cognia — frontend, IPC bridge, Rust backend, and Node sidecar — and how they communicate. Architecture Cognia has four collaborating layers. Picking the right layer for a change is the single most important architectural decision when contributing. Layer 1 — Browser / React Everything in app/, components/, hooks/, and most of lib/ runs inside the webview. This includes: Routes (app/) — Chat workspace, twin workbench, scheduler, agent teams, A2UI, canvas, skills, logs. State — Zustand stores for ephemeral UI state; Dexie (IndexedDB) for persistent data; lib/settings/ for user preferences. AI orchestration — lib/ai/, lib/claude/build-options.ts, lib/twin/runtime/apply-twin-context.ts. Domain logic — lib/character/ (via lib/claude/types.ts), lib/skills/, lib/data/ (backup), … The browser layer has no direct access to OS resources — all native operations go through Layer 2. Provider chain in app/layout.tsx The order of providers in app/layout.tsx matters: 1. ThemeProvider (next-themes) — class-based dark mode driver. 2. LocaleGate — waits for next-intl translations before rendering. 3. SettingsSyncProvider — reads/writes the settings Dexie table. 4. TauriProvider — supplies isTauri() context, OS info, deep-link events. 5. TooltipProvider — Radix; mounted once globally. 6. LoggerProvider — wires the browser logger into the Rust logging bridge. 7. ExternalAgentInitializer, SchedulerInitializer — boot subsystems on first paint. 8. BackupSchedulerProvider — schedules encrypted auto-backups (Tauri only). 9. CanvasBridgeProvider, A2UIDispatchProvider — surface routers for Claude responses. 10. DataAdapterProvider — injects the Dexie adapter into the data-hooks layer. Adding a provider that depends on locale → put it inside LocaleGate. Depends on Tauri → inside TauriProvider. The chain is intentionally deep; do not collapse it. Layer 2 — IPC bridge (lib/tauri.ts) lib/tauri.ts is the single point that calls Tauri's invoke(). Every Rust command has a typed wrapper here. Business code imports named functions from @/lib/tauri, never invoke() directly. isTauri() lets the same component work in both web mode and desktop mode. It returns true only when window. TAURI INTERNALS is present. The wrappers re-export from lib/tauri/index.ts, which groups by plugin (clipboard, dialog, fs, notification, opener, os, process, store, …). en.title: Runtime model & Tauri integration
en.text: How the dual web/desktop runtime works, how to add new IPC commands, and the security boundaries that protect users. Runtime model & Tauri integration Cognia ships a single React codebase that runs in two modes: Web mode — pnpm dev opens the app at http://localhost:3000 in your browser. Desktop mode — pnpm tauri dev opens it inside a Tauri webview with full OS access. Most components work identically in both modes. The few that don't go through lib/tauri.ts. The isTauri() gate Use it to guard any code path that calls a Rust command: In SSR (Next.js server components), isTauri() always returns false because window is undefined. Wrap Tauri-dependent UI in a client component ("use client"). How isTauri() and the IPC bridge fit together The single-invoke rule Only lib/tauri.ts and its sub-modules under lib/tauri/ may call invoke(). Every Rust command gets a typed wrapper: Why this rule: One place to add request validation, error mapping, and telemetry. Business code stays portable — easy to mock in tests. Refactors of the Rust API only touch lib/tauri.ts. If you find a stray invoke() outside this folder during code review, move it. Adding a new IPC command ### Define the command in Rust Add it to src-tauri/src/commands.rs (or a domain-specific module like src-tauri/src/scheduler/commands.rs): Return Result so Tauri serialises errors as a string the JS side can catch. Use String not &str for arguments — Tauri owns its own buffers. For long-running work, take tauri::Window and emit progress events. ### Register it in lib.rs ### Add a typed wrapper in lib/tauri.ts Or place it in a sub-module under lib/tauri/ if the surface is large (e.g., everything scheduler-related lives in lib/tauri/scheduler.ts). ### Write the test Sibling lib/tauri.test.ts. Mock @tauri-apps/api/core: Then assert the wrapper passes the right command name + args. Inline #[cfg(test)] mod tests block: Tauri configuration (src-tauri/tauri.conf.json) Key fields: About the bundle identifier identifier is com.cognia.desktop — a legacy value carried over from the original starter. Tauri uses this string to derive the per-user app data directory . Changing it would orphan every existing installation's settings, vector store, and chat history. For 99% of contributors, leave identifier alone. Tauri-derived per-user data directory by platform: Platform Path -------- ----------------------------------------

en.title: Sidecar & Claude Agent SDK
en.text: How the bundled Node sidecar bridges the Claude Agent SDK to the Tauri parent process, including the JSON-lines protocol, lifecycle, and A2UI MCP. Sidecar & Claude Agent SDK Cognia ships a small Node host (the sidecar ) that wraps the official @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk and exposes it to the Tauri parent process over stdio with a JSON-lines protocol . This page covers what the sidecar does, why, and how to extend it. Why a separate process The Agent SDK has Node-only dependencies (filesystem, child process, native modules) that cannot run inside a webview. Three options were considered: 1. Pure web — call Anthropic's REST API directly from React. Rejected because we lose the SDK's tool-use loop, hooks, MCP integration, and credential discovery. 2. Embed in Rust — talk to Anthropic from Rust. Rejected because the SDK is JS-first and we'd need to reimplement substantial logic. 3. Sidecar — Tauri spawns a Node process; talk to it over stdio. Chosen. The SDK runs unchanged; the Rust side owns lifecycle and credentials. What's in sidecar/ The sidecar is outside the root pnpm workspace because: It needs Node-only deps that conflict with the browser bundle. It ships as a Tauri resource (see tauri.conf.json → bundle.resources) — the entire node modules/ is shipped to users. Versioning is independent of the main app. Protocol: JSON-lines over stdio The Tauri side spawns the sidecar with tauri::api::process::Command. Communication: Each message is one JSON object on its own line , terminated by \n. Parent → sidecar writes go to the sidecar's stdin. Sidecar → parent writes go to stdout. stderr is reserved for sidecar-side logs and is mirrored into the Rust logger. The full protocol is specified in the comment block at the top of claude-host.mjs. The high-level shape: Direction Type Payload --------- ------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------- → init type: "init", apiKey?, workingDir? — set credentials and CWD. → send type: "send", messages, options — start a new turn. ← delta type: "delta", content — streaming token chunks. ← tool use type: "tool use", name, input — model wants to call a tool. → tool result type: "tool result", id, content — tool output. ← done type: "done", usage — turn finished. ← error type: "error", message — fatal error; sidecar exits. → kill type: "kill" — graceful shutdown. options (in send) carries the

en.title: Backup & data transfer
en.text: Schema v3 backup format with AES-GCM encryption, scheduled auto-backups, per-domain transfers, and external chat imports. Backup & data transfer schema v3 AES-GCM-encrypted, integrity-checked backups in package format v3 . Auto-key per-device (no passphrase) or user passphrase for portability. Six per-domain transfers (skills, MCP, presets, characters, teams, theme) let you move just one slice. ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini imports map external exports into Cognia's chat shape. Cognia ships a complete backup / restore / transfer system under lib/data/. The package format is v3 (BackupPackageV3); v1 files import through the migrateEnvelope boundary so legacy users keep working. The full design rationale is in ADR-0001. The external v3 payload keeps the canvasComments field for file compatibility. Runtime storage uses contextComments as the single writable source for Canvas, project, artifact, and workflow comments. Export projects Canvas rows into the legacy field; import maps them idempotently back into contextComments. Where it lives Backup package (schema v3) BackupPackageV3 is a JSON object with three top-level fields: Manifest fields End-to-end backup flow Encryption (AES-GCM, PBKDF2-SHA256-600000) Wrapping a BackupPackageV3 in an EncryptedEnvelopeV1: The manifest is duplicated outside the ciphertext so the user can see what the file contains (timestamp, schema version, flags) without entering the passphrase. encryptBackupPackage(pkg, passphrase, manifest) derives a key from the passphrase via PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations (OWASP 2023 recommendation), then AES-GCM-encrypts the canonical-JSON pkg. Auto-key Most users don't want to memorise a backup passphrase. lib/data/backup-key.ts derives a per-device "auto key" stored in the OS keyring (Tauri only). Auto-encrypted backups are decryptable only on the same device — they are not portable. If the user explicitly sets a passphrase, that takes precedence and the backup is portable. Build a snapshot Built-in characters / skills / teams are filtered out of the payload — they re-seed on import. Only user-created data is included. Apply a snapshot applyBackupPackage(pkg, opts) writes the payload to Dexie under one of three merge strategies: Strategy Behaviour ----------- ------------------------------------- skip Skip rows that already exist (by ID). overwrite Replace existing rows. duplicate Re-key conflict

en.title: Data Hooks
en.text: The DataAdapter abstraction — letting chat components run the same code against Dexie (desktop) or a WebSocket bridge (mobile PWA). Data Hooks lib/data-hooks/ is the "slot" between the chat UI and the persistence layer. It extracts the pattern of components directly calling Dexie (useLiveQuery(() = listCharacters())) behind an interface called DataAdapter, injected via . The desktop gets a Dexie implementation; the mobile PWA will later get a WebSocket bridge implementation — the same component code runs in both forms. types.ts defines the DataAdapter interface (4 reactive use reads + 4 one-off mutations). context.tsx is a React Context plus a set of convenience hooks (useCharacters / useCharacter / useSkillsByIds / usePresets etc.); consumers only need these hooks and are unaware of what sits underneath. dexie-adapter.tsx is the desktop production implementation, directly reusing existing functions from lib/db/ ; reactive reads use useLiveQuery from dexie-react-hooks. All hooks include an SSR guard (typeof window !== "undefined"), making them safe to use under output: "export". Design Motivation The cognia-next desktop app stores data in Dexie (IndexedDB), and chat components read it directly via useLiveQuery(() = listCharacters()). But the mobile PWA cannot replicate Dexie — data stays on the desktop machine, and the phone fetches it over LAN/tunnel via WebSocket. The same ChatHeader / Composer / MessageRenderer should not have two copies of the code. DataAdapter unifies "reactive data fetching + submitting changes" into an interface; the desktop injects a Dexie implementation, the mobile injects a WS implementation, and components neither know nor need to know. Interface Key constraints: The use methods are real React hooks — implementations must trigger the same hooks in the same order on every call (useLiveQuery, etc.). The WS implementation must guarantee this itself. Returning undefined means loading — every implementation returns undefined when data is not yet ready; components uniformly render a "loading" state. Empty collections return [] , not undefined (avoids ambiguity between loading and "empty list"). Mutations do not require awaiting — void adapter.recordPresetUsage(id) is valid usage; the UI uses optimistic updates.
