en.title: Personal Knowledge Capture
en.text: The three modules ADR-0060 introduced together — capture (fingerprint-deduped clippings enriched by the web reader or OCR), the web reader itself (bespoke scrapers ahead of generic extraction), and Attention Radar (a periodic LLM report over what you captured). Personal Knowledge Capture Beta · ADR-0060 · capturedItems v97 · radarReports v96 Three modules that only make sense together. Capture turns a confirmed candidate into a persisted item — dedup by fingerprint, enrich, save (lib/capture/capture-manager.ts). The web reader is what enrichment calls for a URL, and it tries a bespoke scraper before generic extraction, because for a handful of sites a purpose-built scraper beats extraction outright. Attention Radar then runs collect → generate → persist over the accumulated items on an interval, producing an LLM report — with guards that skip the run entirely when there isn't enough new material to be worth the tokens. Design rationale: ADR-0060, which introduced all three in one decision. Capture: fingerprint, enrich, save captureManager takes a confirmed CaptureCandidate and produces a persisted CapturedItem. The fingerprint index on the table (capturedItems: "&id, capturedAt, kind, sourceApp, fingerprint") is what makes dedup a lookup rather than a scan — clipping the same passage twice does not create two items. Enrichment is where a clipping stops being a bare string: a URL goes through the web reader, an image through OCR. enrich.ts takes its dependencies as an injected EnrichDeps, with buildEnrichDeps() as the production wiring — so the manager is testable without a network or an OCR engine. Web reader: bespoke scrapers come first scrapePlatform (lib/web/reader/dispatch.ts) is tried before the generic fetch-and-extract path in web fetch. For WeChat articles, X/Twitter threads and YouTube pages a purpose-built scraper returns clean Markdown that generic extraction cannot match. For everything else it returns null and the caller falls through to local extraction — and if that comes back too thin, to the Jina fallback. That ordering is the whole routing rule: bespoke → local generic → remote fallback, each step only reached because the previous one declined. Attention Radar: guarded, not scheduled-blindly radar-runner.ts orchestrates collect → generate → persist, and it declines to run more often than it should. Two guards mirror the OpenWiki behaviour:

en.title: Long-term Memory
en.text: Durable personal recall — how a fact gets extracted from a conversation, governed by evidence and provenance, retrieved back into a turn, and exposed to plugins, MCP and the companion API without ever letting third-party content rewrite the agent's behavior. Long-term Memory Beta · memories schema v65 → governance v118 → v122 A learned memory is a durable fact inferred from a conversation or deliberately saved by the user. Write goes through one funnel — storeMemoryCore() (lib/memory/api/store-memory.ts:78) — and read through another — retrieveMemories() (packages/memory/src/retrieve/retriever.ts:266), which applyMemoryContext() (packages/memory/src/runtime/apply-memory-context.ts:102) folds into the turn. What keeps it safe is provenance : only user / explicit memories may ever be procedural, so an inbound connector message cannot silently rewrite how the agent behaves. Everything durable lives in four Dexie tables — memories plus the immutable memoryEvidence, the durable memoryJobs queue, and the content-free memoryAuditEvents — introduced together at schema v118 . The design rationale is in ADR-0069. This page documents the current implementation. The domain vocabulary — and the distinctions the product deliberately keeps separate — is maintained in lib/memory/CONTEXT.md. What is and isn't a memory The subsystem is strict about this, because collapsing these categories is how a recall system turns into an unaccountable policy engine: Concept Owned by Becomes learned memory? --- --- --- Learned memory this subsystem it is one — recall context, not enforced policy Human instruction user / team / admin, with an explicit author and precedence no Task checkpoint a task or conversation lifecycle only by explicit promotion Procedure a Skill or Workflow no — procedures load on demand Team blackboard agents coordinating on one run no — short-lived run state External context tools, MCP, web search, connectors, screen capture no — it is evidence , with its own trust level A turn whose answer depended on external context is a contaminated turn . It may use learned memory, but it does not create it automatically — reviewed evidence still has to be promoted explicitly. Where it lives The core was extracted into @cognia/memory so it builds standalone; types/memory/memory.ts is a boundary shim re-exporting @cognia/memory/types/memory, which keeps 80 existing importers un

en.title: Authoring and SDK
en.text: Public manifest, Code 1.128 catalog, providers, protocols, and deterministic proxy generation. Authoring and SDK Authors declare only manifest.ide: The generator locks the live Code 1.128 extension schema and every referenced schema in packages/plugin-sdk/contract/code-1.128-contribution-schemas.json. Exact upstream digests and provenance are checked before generation. The resulting code-1.128-ide.json catalog hash is part of broker negotiation and proxy activation. The generated public JSON Schema is self-contained and has no external references. The build emits TypeScript types/helpers, JSON Schema, normalized engine-neutral IR, exhaustive conformance fixtures, and proxy contribution metadata. An unclassified stable contribution or provider fails generation. Legacy vscode author fields are normalized with field-level deprecation diagnostics for one major; generated SDK output uses only manifest.ide. Global IDs are rewritten to cognia. . . Duplicate, reserved, or externally occupied IDs reject the entire activation transaction. Static assets are canonical plugin-relative files. A plugin cannot provide an extension entrypoint. Proxy VSIX output is deterministic and content-addressed. Its Ed25519-signed descriptor binds plugin id/version, manifest hash, platform version, catalog hash, executable resource hashes, and VSIX digest. codeserver build proxy only stages the artifact; codeserver activate proxy promotes it after a live handshake. The activation marker, not the artifact cache, is authoritative on restart. Stable provider coverage includes language features and virtual filesystems; views, trees, status, decorations, webviews and custom editors; terminals, tasks, SCM, debug, tests, notebooks and comments; authentication, URI handling and storage; Chat participants, language-model tools, MCP definitions, and the stable contribution families in the locked catalog.

en.title: Compatibility and release gates
en.text: Supported versions, hosts, exclusions, protocol compatibility, and stable-release verification. Compatibility and release gates Host Architecture Result --- --- --- Linux amd64 / arm64 supported macOS amd64 / arm64 supported Windows any unsupported platform; no npm fallback This release pins code-server 4.128.0 and Code 1.128.0. An upgrade requires an upstream catalog diff, schema import digest refresh, generator changes, compatibility fixtures, and real E2E approval. Remote hosts must preload the matching binary; mismatch returns REMOTE CODE SERVER UPGRADE REQUIRED. Proposed/internal VS Code APIs, remote-authority implementations, extension-management APIs, Windows hosts, and third-party extensionDependencies in managed profile return structured compatibility errors. They never silently no-op. Stable release requires catalog-entry conformance, malformed/oversized frame and cancellation-race tests, stale-generation and reconnect tests, path and ticket security tests, profile isolation, deterministic proxy/update rollback, offline artifacts, two-major negotiation, and real local/paired E2E for LSP, DAP, MCP, SCM, tests, notebooks, webviews/custom editors, and Chat flows. Performance gates are: cold readiness regression at most 20% and 2 seconds; idle RSS regression at most 20% and 150 MiB; local empty broker RPC p95 at most 30 ms; remote relay overhead excluding physical RTT p95 at most 75 ms; and no control/lifecycle event loss within declared capacity. Remote telemetry is opt-in and aggregate-only. Source, paths, prompts, arguments, environments, secrets, and content handles never enter telemetry.

en.title: Managed IDE Extension Platform
en.text: Architecture and ownership map for Cognia-managed Monaco and Pro IDE extensions. Managed IDE Extension Platform Protocol 1.0 · Code 1.128.0 · code-server 4.128.0 The platform projects one Cognia plugin runtime into Monaco and Pro IDE. A Pro IDE proxy contains validated declarations, static assets, and platform-owned bootstrap code; plugin business code never runs in the VS Code extension host. Each host owns two mutually exclusive profiles. Managed Pro IDE loads pinned built-ins, the Cognia broker, and signed generated proxies. Native Extensions IDE loads user-selected Open VSX extensions in a separate process, port, user-data-dir, and extensions-dir; it never receives broker credentials. The profiles do not share extension state, secrets, Workspace Trust, or capability tickets. The platform is split into four planes: Authoring and SDK: manifest.ide, the locked catalog, schema, provider families, and proxy generation. Protocol and security: framing, authentication, authorization, storage, webviews, and protocol processes. Operations: local/remote hosting, transactional updates, migration, Dev Mode, and troubleshooting. Compatibility: version policy, explicit exclusions, and release gates. ADR context remains in ADR-0088.

en.title: Operations, updates, and troubleshooting
en.text: Local and paired hosting, transactional updates, migration, Dev Mode, and recovery. Operations, updates, and troubleshooting Local operation stays in Tauri. For a paired host, code-server, profiles, plugins, permissions, secrets, proxies, and protocol processes run on the remote Cognia host. The desktop does not upgrade that binary. It reaches the remote workbench through a local ephemeral relay that pins the paired certificate SPKI fingerprint, then sends the existing device JWT in an Authorization header. The real remote port and credentials stay loopback-only. The relay is mounted on the companion front door at /ide/relay/ / (protocol/companion-api-routes.json) behind require device access, so the credential it forwards is an ordinary device access token — the same one every other device request carries. Those live five minutes, and only the renderer holds the device private key needed to mint one, so lib/codeserver/remote-relay.ts re-mints ahead of expiry and re-ensures the relay. A re-ensure for the same host, path and fingerprint swaps the token in place and keeps the bound port: rebinding would hand the webview a new URL and reboot the workbench, losing exactly the session the pane exists to protect. Plugin updates use a durable transaction: 1. plugin stage version downloads and verifies checksum/signature, extracts into host-owned transaction storage, validates the manifest and resources, and leaves the working package untouched. 2. The renderer validates permission expansion and the declarative migration plan, then stages the deterministic proxy. 3. The host snapshots the old package and .host-state, including managed IDE SQLite state and secret indexes. 4. The old runtime is disabled/unloaded and plugin commit staged update atomically renames the staged package into place. 5. The exact staged proxy is activated. The code-server host attempts live activation first, restarts only the extension host when required, and restores the old proxy on handshake failure. 6. Runtime verification succeeds before the transaction is finalized. A failure after commit restores package and host state, rescans the runtime, and re-enables the old version. A full Pro IDE restart is offered only when the old package/state are confirmed restored but old runtime activation still cannot complete. Uncommitted artifacts have no activation marker and are ignored on code-server

en.title: Protocol and security
en.text: Broker negotiation, callback authorization, storage, content handles, webviews, and process supervision. Protocol and security Protocol 1.0 is JSON-RPC 2.0 over loopback TCP with Content-Length framing. Frames, headers, queues, handles, in-flight requests, and deadlines are bounded. Challenge/HMAC authentication proves possession of a per-instance secret without placing it in the hello. The hello negotiates protocol major, Code API version, catalog hash, host, canonical workspace, and capabilities. Each connection has a monotonic generation. Disconnect fails all pending requests. Responses, cancellation, progress, events, content handles, and tickets from an old generation are rejected. Reconnect rebuilds registrations, subscriptions, and snapshots only; actions are never replayed. Protocol majors 1 and its predecessor are supported through negotiation. The legacy 0.2.x newline bridge remains compatibility-only for one release and reports new capabilities as unsupported. Large or binary values use one-shot 30-second content handles bound to root, generation, plugin, provider, permission, and direction. Bytes move through a separate authenticated loopback endpoint; credentials never appear in URLs. Every callback revalidates the canonical host/root, workspace trust, current generation, plugin enabled/version state, declaration, provider handler, permission decision, and contextual ticket when required. Shell, debug, test, notebook execution, external writes, and agent tools require contextual confirmation. File paths and URIs are canonicalized on the IDE host; missing descendants resolve through their deepest existing ancestor and symlink escape fails closed. Managed state lives in host-owned SQLite outside plugin-writable directories. Global state, workspace state, and secrets are partitioned by user, host, plugin, workspace, and area. State partitions have a 5 MiB quota. Secret values stay in the OS keyring; SQLite stores only the partitioned key index. secrets:read and secrets:write are rechecked on each operation. Proxy-local state is a rebuildable cache, and secrets are never cached. Webviews use default-src 'none', typed messages, and content-addressed resources. File, command, network, and secret operations return through broker authorization. Protocol executables must be signed plugin resources, registered host tools, or an executable explicitly selec

en.title: A2UI MCP Bridge
en.text: The a2ui-bridge MCP server in both forms — the in-process SDK server mounted every session and the standalone a2ui-mcp.mjs stdio server for external CLIs. Five tools from one source of truth (tool-defs.mjs), the buildDispatch mapping, the COGNIA BRIDGE SOCKET IPC path, graceful detached-mode degradation, and the fifth tool (a2ui handle connector action) that lets IM users drive surfaces. A2UI MCP Bridge Stable · 5 tools · single source tool-defs.mjs · in-process + standalone The a2ui-bridge lets an agent draw interactive UI through MCP. It exists in two forms that share one contract: an in-process SDK server (a2ui-tools/index.mjs, mounted by the sidecar every session, alwaysLoad: true) and a standalone stdio server (a2ui-mcp.mjs, spawned by external CLIs like Claude Code or Cursor and talking JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout). Both pull their five tool names, descriptions, schemas, and dispatch mapping from a single module — sidecar/a2ui-tools/tool-defs.mjs — so the two servers can never drift (a Node test asserts the contract). The in-process form emit()s a dispatch event; the standalone form writes it to the COGNIA BRIDGE SOCKET Unix socket / named pipe. Both converge on the renderer's A2UI store. The fifth tool, a2ui handle connector action, injects an IM user's action onto a surface so browser-side and chat-side users share one flow. One source, two servers Tool Dispatch type Purpose ---- ------------- ------- a2ui create surface createSurface open a surface (inline / dialog / panel / fullscreen) a2ui update components updateComponents replace the component tree (A2UI v0.9 schema) a2ui data model update dataModelUpdate patch/replace form values, chart data, table rows a2ui delete surface deleteSurface remove a surface, free resources a2ui handle connector action connectorAction inject an IM-channel user action onto a surface tool-defs.mjs exports TOOL NAMES, TOOL DESCRIPTIONS, RAW INPUT SCHEMAS (JSON Schema), a rawTools() helper, and buildDispatch(name, args) — the function both servers use to turn tool args into a dispatch envelope: A drift-guard test pins the contract: The renderer keeps a parallel typed copy in lib/a2ui/mcp-tool-schemas.ts (A2UI BRIDGE TOOLS, line 53) used to seed the built-in a2ui-bridge row (buildA2UIBridgeMcpRow, line 197), to detect that row (isA2UIBridgeRow), and to compute its namespaced tool names for projection to external agents. en.title: Agent Sync & Health
en.text: Durable Agent projection, sidecar Runtime Gateway discovery, guarded remote Anthropic relays, and persisted per-server operations in the MCP Health view. Agent Sync & Health Stable · durable mcpSyncJobs · sidecar Runtime Gateway · mcpAuditLog (10k / 30d) Each McpServer row carries an appsEnabled matrix mapping AgentId → boolean. When you flip a chip, the CRUD layer debounces a write of that server into the agent's on-disk MCP config (lib/claude/sync). Because files can drift from Cognia's view (hand-edits, failed syncs), use-agent-status computes per-agent drift — missing (projected but absent from file) and unmanaged (in file, unknown to Cognia) — surfaced by the drift banner with a one-click re-sync. The test button uses the sidecar Runtime Gateway for guarded capability discovery. The Health tab combines live runtime counters with persisted per-server failure rate, connect p95, capability freshness, Agent sync lag, inbound External-Bridge status, and the content-free mcpAuditLog. The projection matrix Seven agents are writable (Cognia mirrors servers into their config) and two are read-only (adapters that don't write — Cognia can read their config but not push): A chip toggle patches appsEnabled[agent] in Dexie; the CRUD layer schedules the file sync: Chip states (mcp-agent-chip-group.tsx:4): on (projected here), off (file exists, not projected), missing (no file — inert), readonly (adapter can't write — inert). Drift detection use-agent-status reads each agent's config file through an adapter and diffs the in-file server names against Cognia's projections: missing — the actionable kind; the drift banner shows a Re-sync button (syncToAgent). unmanaged — informational (hand-rolled entries); the banner offers Import instead. The drift banner (components/settings/mcp-drift-banner.tsx) only renders for agents with missing.length 0, is per-session dismissible, and expands to list the offending server names: The agent status bar (mcp-agent-status-bar.tsx) is the Agents-tab header: per-agent file path, in-file count vs projected count (amber when they disagree), and a per-agent + a sync-all button. Sidecar Runtime Gateway discovery The Test button and workflow tool picker call discoverMcpServerViaSidecar. The trusted host checks policy and resolves SecretRef values, then the allowlisted mcp-discover feature call reaches sidecar/dispatch/mcp-runtime-gateway.mjs.

en.title: Built-in Tools (cognia-tools)
en.text: The in-process cognia-tools MCP server the sidecar mounts every session — 44 tools across 7 categories (file-extras, git, process, environment, shell-advanced, terminal-repl, lsp), the safety.mjs layer (path-traversal guard, command allow/blocklist, dangerous-pattern scan), the metadata-driven toggles, and the plugin-tools proxy bridge. Built-in Tools (cognia-tools) Stable · 44 tools · 7 categories · safety-gated sidecar/builtin-tools/index.mjs:buildCogniaToolsServer assembles an in-process SDK MCP server named cognia-tools from per-category tool modules — fileExtras (13), git (9), process (9), environment (3), shellAdvanced (1), terminalRepl (4), and lsp (5, dynamic) — 44 tools total, namespaced mcp cognia-tools . Categories are gated by settings.builtinTools. toggles, and disabled categories are also pushed to disallowedTools as defence-in-depth. Every tool routes through safety.mjs: a path-traversal guard, a shell allowlist/blocklist + dangerous-pattern scanner, secret redaction, and the toolText/toolError result wrappers. Write/exec tools (directory delete, start process, terminate process, shell execute advanced) are HIGH-RISK and always pass through the SDK canUseTool approval gate. Assembly buildCogniaToolsServer( enabled, alwaysLoad, lspResolver ) (line 69) includes only enabled categories, binds the LSP tools to the per-session resolver when present, and returns null when nothing is enabled (so the dispatch layer can skip mounting). Category IDs, tool names, server name, and version come from a shared JSON (lib/settings/builtin-tools-data.json) so the React settings UI and the sidecar never drift. Disabled categories are blocked twice — not mounted, and their tool names are added to disallowedTools: Tool reference Namespace: mcp cognia-tools . en.title: Consumption Surfaces
en.text: The places outside the main settings panel that consume MCP config — the agent custom-mode tool selector (budget + AI recommendations), the scheduler server picker (default vs explicit), the CCSwitch import tab, the chat transcript tool-card renderer registry, and the A2UI bridge settings tab. Consumption Surfaces Stable · 5 surfaces across agent / scheduler / chat / settings Beyond the settings panel, five surfaces read the MCP config in different shapes. The tool selector (agent custom modes) picks individual tools under a budget, with AI-ranked recommendations. The scheduler picker picks whole servers, distinguishing "use defaults" (undefined) from "explicitly none" ([]). The CCSwitch tab is a second importer, pulling MCP configs from CCSwitch-managed CLIs into the mcpServers store. The chat tool-card registry maps tool names to bespoke result cards (wiki/rag/read/plan/grep…) with a generic fallback. The A2UI bridge tab controls the always-on a2ui-bridge row's per-agent projection and shows live bridge health. Tool selector components/agent/mode/custom-mode-editor/mcp-tool-selector.tsx lets a custom mode enable a specific subset of MCP tools under a budget. It reads connected servers + their tools from the useMcpStore stub and the budget from toolSelectionConfig, asks getRecommendedMcpToolsForMode for AI-ranked picks from the mode's metadata, and emits McpToolReference[] ( serverId, toolName, displayName ): An over-budget badge warns when the selection exceeds toolSelectionConfig.maxTools; an "Apply Recommended" button fills the selection from the recommendations panel. Scheduler picker components/scheduler/payload-editors/mcp-picker.tsx picks servers (not tools) for a scheduled task. Its key subtlety is the two-state value — an empty array means "explicitly disable MCP", undefined means "let resolveSendOptions pick the character/team default": A radio toggles default vs custom; in custom mode a checklist of listMcpServers() (disabled rows filtered out) drives the id array. CCSwitch MCP tab components/settings/ccswitch/tabs/mcp-tab.tsx is a second importer (alongside the import dialog). It reads MCP servers that CCSwitch manages for external CLIs and imports the picks with a collision strategy: Desktop-only (a web-mode alert otherwise); each row shows transport + notes; strategy is a radio. See the CCSwitch subsystem for the propagation side of this sync.

en.title: Overview
en.text: Cognia's complete Model Context Protocol surface — how it consumes external MCP servers (config store, presets, per-session resolution), mirrors them to external coding agents, and the in-process servers the sidecar hosts (cognia-tools built-ins + the a2ui-bridge). One config model (Dexie mcpServers) drives chat, scheduler, agent modes, and seven external CLIs. MCP System Governed · Dexie schema v151 · 3 transports · scoped runtime Cognia wears four MCP faces . As a client , it stores user/plugin/built-in server definitions in one Dexie table (mcpServers) and resolves a per-turn subset into the Claude Agent SDK's mcpServers option (build-options.ts:resolveSendOptions → buildMcpServerMap). As a mirror , it projects each server's appsEnabled matrix into the on-disk config of seven external CLIs (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, Gemini, Windsurf, plus read-only Cline/Roo-Code) and watches for drift. As a host , the sidecar mounts two in-process SDK MCP servers per session — cognia-tools (44 built-in tools across 7 categories, gated by safety.mjs) and a2ui-bridge (5 surface tools). As a server for outsiders , Cognia exposes its own knowledge + action surface over stdio/HTTP — that plane lives in the External Bridge subsystem. This section documents the first three faces. Raw credentials are replaced with SecretRef values and resolved only inside the trusted host: New/manual/imported/plugin definitions start pending, disabled, and unprojected. en.title: Presets & Import
en.text: Where MCP server rows come from — the 15 built-in presets (lib/claude/mcp-presets.ts) with their field-substitution engine, the plugin overlay registry that lets plugins contribute presets, the blank-server seed that pre-projects to all writable agents, and the three-step import dialog that pulls servers out of existing CLI config files. Presets & Import Stable · 15 built-in presets · plugin overlay · CLI import Most users never type a stdio command by hand. The Preset Market ships 15 curated presets (MCP PRESETS, lib/claude/mcp-presets.ts:46) — filesystem, github, postgres, slack, deepwiki, and generic http/sse — each declaring typed fields (env vars, arg tokens, URLs, headers) that applyPresetFields substitutes into a config blob. Every path lands in the same mcpServers row. en.title: Server Config & Store
en.text: The McpServer config model and its Dexie store — the transport union (stdio/http/sse), the config payload shapes, the mcpServers table (id·name·enabled, since v2), the CRUD layer that fires agent-sync side effects, buildMcpServerMap for the SDK, and the UI projection helpers. Server Config & Store Stable · lib/db/mcp-servers.ts · 211 lines One Dexie table, mcpServers, holds every MCP server definition. Its row type (McpServer, lib/claude/types.ts:1969) carries a transport discriminator and a transport-shaped config blob (stdio → command, args?, env? ; http/sse → url, headers? ). mcp-servers.ts is the CRUD layer: every create/update/delete bumps updatedAt and fires a fire-and-forget scheduleSyncFor(appsEnabled) so the change is mirrored to the relevant external-CLI config files. buildMcpServerMap projects reviewed rows into the Agent SDK namespace. Settings discovery resolves SecretRef values only in the trusted host, then uses the sidecar Runtime Gateway; no renderer-owned MCP SDK or native hand-written probe remains. The config model The config payload is transport-shaped , never normalized into typed columns: Transport config shape Probe / SDK key --------- -------------- --------------- stdio command: string, args?: string[], env?: Record spawns a child process http url: string, headers?: Record streamable-HTTP POST sse url: string, headers?: Record legacy SSE endpoint types/mcp/index.ts carries only small re-export stubs used by migrated agent code — McpServerStatus ("stopped" "starting" "running" "error" "unknown"), McpServerInfo, and McpToolSelectionConfig (the budget/allowlist shape consumed by the tool selector). The Dexie table mcpServers was introduced in Dexie v2 and its index signature has been stable ever since (lib/db/schema.ts:332, repeated unchanged through later versions): Primary key id (string) — O(1) get. Index name — ordered listing for the panel. Index enabled — fast filter for listEnabledMcpServers. The v7 upgrade added the appsEnabled per-agent projection field and backfilled onto legacy rows so downstream code never has to null-check. CRUD layer lib/db/mcp-servers.ts is the only writer. Every mutation bumps updatedAt and schedules an agent sync. en.title: Session Resolution
en.text: How a stored MCP server becomes a live tool in one chat turn — the resolveSendOptions precedence chain (member › character › team › all) plus tool filters, buildMcpServerMap, the builtin-mcp placeholder resolver that injects the bridge socket for external agents, and the sidecar dispatch that merges user + cognia-tools + a2ui-bridge + plugin-tools before query(). Session Resolution Stable · build-options.ts + builtin-mcp/ + dispatch/anthropic.mjs Resolution happens in two stages. Renderer side (build-options.ts:resolveSendOptions) decides which enabled servers this turn gets, walking a precedence chain — a team-member override beats the character's mcpServerIds, which beats the team's, which falls back to all enabled — then applies any tool filter, and projects the survivors through buildMcpServerMap into opts.mcpServers. Sidecar side (dispatch/anthropic.mjs) takes that map and layers the in-process servers on top: cognia-tools (built-ins), a2ui-bridge (always-loaded), and cognia-plugin-tools (when present), each with a name-shadow guard. For external agents, a third helper (builtin-mcp/resolve.ts) rewrites $ COGNIA SIDECAR DIR placeholders and injects the COGNIA BRIDGE SOCKET env so the a2ui-bridge child can phone home. Stage 1 — which servers (renderer) resolveSendOptions (lib/claude/build-options.ts:931) resolves the per-turn subset. The precedence is strict — the first matching tier wins: Tier Source When ---- ------ ---- 1 memberOverride.mcpServerIdsOverride team chat, per-member 2 character.mcpServerIds a character pins a subset 3 team.mcpServerIds team session default 4 all enabled servers nothing above is set A configurable tool filter then narrows further — allow intersects, deny subtracts: The output is opts.mcpServers: Record — see buildMcpServerMap. This rides SendOptions into the sidecar. Stage 2 — placeholder resolution (external agents) Built-in MCP rows (notably the projected a2ui-bridge row) ship placeholder tokens instead of absolute paths, because the bundle location is only known at runtime. builtin-mcp/resolve.ts rewrites them. Two operations: substitute $ COGNIA SIDECAR DIR across command/args/env, and — for the a2ui-bridge row only — inject COGNIA BRIDGE SOCKET so the spawned child can dispatch back to the renderer: The substitution avoids regex so Windows backslashes never need escaping: The runtime paths come from Rust over IPC and a

en.title: Network Proxy
en.text: One outbound policy for the desktop Host — Off / Manual / Auto over HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS5, enforced in Rust so no renderer path can dial around it. Network Proxy Stable · desktop Host · keyring credentials Settings → Network configures one proxy for the desktop Host : the Tauri renderer, the Rust core, the WebSocket and streaming bridges it owns, and the child processes it spawns that are allowed to reach the network. The renderer never decides direct-vs-proxy and never sees the password — every request crosses into Rust, where apply reqwest policy applies the mode, the bypass list and the keyring credential. audit:network-egress keeps it that way: a new bare fetch, new WebSocket, or reqwest::Client::new() fails the build unless it is declared, one file at a time, with a reason. Scope: the desktop Host, and nothing else The setting says "route every outbound request" and it means every request this desktop app makes. Three things are deliberately outside it: The browser build. A page in a browser tab uses the browser's own proxy settings; a web app cannot override them, and pretending otherwise would be a lie in the UI. The Capacitor mobile shell. Same reasoning — the OS owns the route. The companion transport. lib/tauri/pinned-fetch.ts and its socket pin a TLS fingerprint against a device the user paired with directly. Re-routing that through a proxy would break the pin it exists to check. Why every request crosses into Rust The packaged shell serves the renderer under a static CSP whose connect-src is 'self' ipc: http://ipc.localhost ws: wss:. There is no http: or https: scheme in it, so a renderer fetch("https://api.example.com") is blocked before it leaves the WebView — and http://127.0.0.1:11434 is blocked too, because loopback is not 'self'. pnpm dev runs without a CSP. That gap is the whole problem: a bare fetch looks perfectly healthy in development and is dead in the packaged app. It has shipped that way repeatedly — the OTLP and Langfuse log transports, the entire local-provider surface, web search, RAG reranking, cloud OCR, and a Site preview readiness probe that had been polling a dev server it could never reach. Even where a request is not blocked, a renderer fetch never sees the proxy: the mode, the bypass list and the keyring password all live in crates/cognia-net/src/proxy config/. en.title: Agent-Trace Spans
en.text: The lib/agent-trace span pipeline — the OTel-GenAI-aligned AgentTraceSpan model, the in-memory emitter (start/event/end), who produces spans (chat turn, tool calls, team hand-off, plugin hooks, workflow LLM nodes), and the converters to StructuredLogEntry and OTLP/HTTP JSON. The shared spine that feeds both the log panel and the tracing dashboard. Agent-Trace Spans Agent-trace is a pure-TS span pipeline. lib/agent-trace/emitter.ts buffers in-progress spans in a Map ; startSpan → recordEvent → endSpan hands the finished span to a registered writer. lib/logging/bootstrap.ts wires that writer to dispatchSpanToTransports, which converts the span to a StructuredLogEntry (spanToLogEntry) and fans it to the transports — the agent-trace transport persists it to the Dexie agentTraces table, and the otlp-http transport exports it to /v1/traces. Spans are OTel-GenAI shaped (gen ai. semconv). Producers: every chat turn (invoke agent), each tool call (execute tool child), team hand-offs, plugin hooks, and workflow LLM nodes. Consumers: the log panel's Traces channel and the tracing dashboard. The Span Model AgentTraceSpan (types/agent-trace/span.ts:65) is the persisted row — short JS-friendly field names, with the OTel mapping deferred to the OTLP converter: AGENT TRACE SPAN KIND = "agent-trace-span" (span.ts:120) is the discriminator embedded in StructuredLogEntry.data so transports can recognise span-shaped entries. The Dexie agentTraces table (v55) is indexed by id(pk), sessionId, [sessionId+startTime], traceId, [traceId+startTime], parentSpanId, and surface. The Emitter endSpan (emitter.ts:165) is idempotent and never throws into the caller — a writer error is swallowed: emitFinishedSpan(partial) (emitter.ts:206) is the one-shot form for self-measured work (plugin hooks use it). generateTraceId() (16 bytes) / generateSpanId() (8 bytes) produce the hex ids. setAgentTraceWriter(fn) registers the sink — wired in lib/logging/bootstrap.ts:660 to dispatchSpanToTransports. The Pipeline Producers Spans are seeded at curated boundaries (the same philosophy as the perf hotspot registry): Producer Span Call site --- --- --- Chat turn invoke agent / anthropic / chat; traceId+spanId echoed into SendOptions hooks/chat/use-claude-chat.ts:855 (start), :1534 (success), :1257 (turn error) Chat tool calls execute tool children parented under the turn chat-tool-spans.ts:138 via handleSd

en.title: Crash Reporting
en.text: src-tauri/src/crash — two capture paths (in-process Rust panic hook writing .txt+.json, and an out-of-process minidump monitor for native hard-crashes), gated by a clean-exit sentinel that drives the next-launch dialog. Includes the CrashReport model, the redacted breadcrumb context, the host snapshot reused by perf, and the seven crash commands. Crash Reporting src-tauri/src/crash/ captures two failure classes. Rust panics are caught in-process by a std::panic::set hook (panic hook.rs) that writes a Minecraft-style .txt plus a structured .json. Native hard-crashes (SIGSEGV, stack overflow, abort, WebView2) are caught out-of-process: a sibling monitor process owns a minidumper::Server, and the app installs a crash handler::CrashHandler that requests a .dmp on fault. Whether the next launch shows a crash dialog is decided not by the presence of a report but by a clean-exit sentinel (.session-running) — written on start, deleted on graceful shutdown — so recoverable worker panics never raise a false alarm. Reports live in /Cognia/crash-reports/. Seven crash commands cover context ingestion, listing/reading/deleting, and consuming the pending-crash signal. The Two Capture Paths The Panic Hook panic hook.rs installs a global hook (idempotent, chains the previous hook) that captures payload, location, thread name, and a forced backtrace, then writes a report and emits crash://captured: write report gathers message/location/thread/backtrace plus system info::gather(), context::snapshot(), and app extra(), builds a CrashReport kind: Panic, … , and writes both files. Recoverable panics (e.g. the automation worker's catch unwind) still write a report here but do not raise the dialog — that's the sentinel's job. The Minidump Monitor monitor.rs runs a sibling process. maybe run monitor() (called first in main.rs) scans argv for --crash-monitor ; if present it runs the minidumper::Server loop and returns so main exits without booting the app. Otherwise install client() spawns the monitor child, connects, and attaches the native handler: On a fault the monitor writes .dmp (create minidump file) and a companion .txt/.json (write companion) built from the last KIND META context forwarded from the app, then exits. The Sentinel — Source of Truth sentinel.rs is what actually decides "did we crash?". A marker file is written on start and deleted on graceful shutdown; surviving

W3C performance.mark/measure helpers under the workflow-ai namespace, the opt-in on-screen PerfHud (PerformanceObserver + p50/p95 + FPS), and the React.Profiler boundary that emits one measure per commit. Frontend Perf Timing lib/perf is a small dev/opt-in instrumentation layer for the browser — completely separate from the Rust performance dashboard. perf-marker.ts wraps the standard W3C performance.mark/measure API (namespaced workflow-ai:) so timings show up in Chrome DevTools and can be aggregated. perf-hud.tsx is a floating HUD that subscribes to those measures via a PerformanceObserver, aggregates p50/p95 per name, and adds a rAF FPS counter — gated behind localStorage.cogniaPerfHud="1" (auto-mounts in dev). profiler-boundary.tsx wraps children in a React.Profiler (non-prod only) and emits one performance.measure per commit, surfacing as react: rows in the HUD. W3C Marker API perf-marker.ts emits standard User-Timing entries, feature-detected and SSR-safe (every call is wrapped in try/catch): All names are prefixed workflow-ai: (PERF NAMESPACE). measureRange(name, startTime, endTime) is the options-object form used by the profiler boundary. clearMeasuresByName(name) drains the User-Timing buffer so it can't grow unbounded. en.title: Observability
en.text: The full observability surface of cognia-next — a unified logging pipeline (browser fan-out + Rust fern dispatch + native OS log bridges), an agent-trace span pipeline, a Langfuse-style tracing dashboard, the Rust performance dashboard (ADR-0035), native crash reporting, and token/cost usage tracking. Two routes (/logs, /performance) plus a next-launch crash dialog. Observability Cognia's observability is five cooperating planes , not one log box. (1) Logging — createLogger("module") enters a single browser pipeline (lib/logging/core.ts:404: level-gate → sample → context-merge → redact → fan-out) that writes to up to 9 transports; the Rust side (src-tauri/src/logging/) takes the same records through fern + tauri-plugin-log into the OS logger (Windows Event Log / macOS os log / Linux journald). (2) Agent-trace — lib/agent-trace/emitter.ts emits OTel-GenAI-shaped spans for every chat turn, tool call, team hand-off, plugin hook, and workflow LLM node; they persist to the Dexie agentTraces table and can Grafana/Langfuse-style draggable panel grid (lib/observability/ is a real percentile/bucketing/rollup engine) reading those spans, over the same window and the same filters as the trace list beside it. (4) Performance — app/performance (ADR-0035) is a Task-Manager-style live view of the Rust process tree, Tokio runtime, and span hotspots, sampled at 1 Hz over perf://sample. (5) Crash reporting — src-tauri/src/crash/ captures Rust panics in-process and native hard-crashes out-of-process (minidump), gated by a clean-exit sentinel . Token/cost usage (lib/claude/usage.ts, Anthropic quota probes, inbox telemetry) rounds out the picture. What It Is "Observability" in cognia-next is everything that answers "what is the app doing, and what went wrong" — across the browser runtime, the Tauri Rust backend, the bundled Node sidecar, plugins, and external agents. Because the app ships as a static export wrapped by Tauri and Capacitor, the design splits cleanly: anything that needs an OS-level capability (a real log file, the Windows Event Log, a minidump handler, the process tree) lives in Rust; the browser owns the unified entry point, the IndexedDB persistence, and the dashboards. The two halves meet over a small set of Tauri commands and events. The five planes are independent enough to read in any order, but they share a spine: structured records with a traceId . A logge

en.title: Logging Pipeline
en.text: The browser-side unified logging core in lib/logging — createLogger entry points, the StructuredLogEntry contract, the core.ts hot path (level-gate → sample → context-merge → normalize → redact → fan-out), per-module sampling, PII redaction, trace-id context, the recent-error ring buffer, and the bootstrap that registers all transports from localStorage. Logging Pipeline Every browser-side log goes through one funnel. createLogger("module") (lib/logging/core.ts:713) returns a CoreLogger; calling .info/.warn/.error/... reaches the private hot path CoreLogger.log (core.ts:404), which: (1) gates on minLevel via LEVEL PRIORITY, (2) asks logSampler.shouldLog (errors/fatals always pass), (3) merges the ambient logContext + per-logger context + call data and lifts correlation fields out, (4) builds a StructuredLogEntry, (5) normalizeEntry (Dates→ISO, Errors→plain), (6) redactStructuredLogEntry, (7) dispatchEntry fans out to every registered transport with per-transport try/catch isolation. The default logger and 25 pre-made loggers. modules all share this funnel — createLogger only tags the module label. Entry Points lib/logging/index.ts exposes three consumption patterns, all of which feed the same core: The 25 pre-made modules (index.ts:133-159): app · ai · chat · agent · mcp · plugin · native · ui · store · network · auth · error · media · scheduler · search · document · export · skills · sync · screenshot · tts · shell · canvas · a2ui · tray. app reuses the singleton logger; the other 24 are fresh createLogger(...) calls. log (index.ts:164) is a shorthand delegating to the default logger. The module tag is the only thing createLogger changes — routing, sampling, and transports are global. The Log Entry Contract StructuredLogEntry (types/logging/log-entry.ts:10) is the single object that flows through the whole pipeline: LEVEL PRIORITY (types/logging/log-level.ts:29) maps trace:0, debug:1, info:2, warn:3, error:4, fatal:5 ; every minLevel comparison and the recent-error filter rely on it. en.title: Performance Dashboard
en.text: ADR-0035 — the Task-Manager-style /performance panel backed by the Rust perf subsystem. Three data layers (process tree via sysinfo, Tokio RuntimeMetrics, an opt-in span-hotspot registry with a log-bucket p50/p95 histogram), a ref-counted 1 Hz sampler over perf://sample, and the four-tab dashboard with its start→backfill→subscribe stream. Performance Dashboard /performance (ADR-0035) is a live, Task-Manager-style view of the Rust runtime — desktop-only. The Rust subsystem src-tauri/src/perf/ composes three layers into a PerfSample 1 Hz over the perf://sample event: (1) the process tree (process.rs) via sysinfo, walking the PID tree from the app down to every descendant, classified main/sidecar/child, CPU normalized to 0–100; (2) the Tokio runtime (runtime.rs) via RuntimeMetrics, headline worker-busy % by diffing monotonic busy durations; (3) span hotspots (registry.rs + span.rs) — a process-global registry where each instrumented &'static str accumulates count/error/total/min/max plus a fixed log-bucket histogram for approximate p50/p95. The sampler is ref-counted — zero cost while the panel is closed. The frontend (hooks/perf/use-perf-stream.ts + components/performance/) starts → backfills from a 120-sample ring → subscribes, and renders four tabs: Overview, Processes, Hotspots, Async Runtime. Why It Exists The app already had logging, crash reporting, frontend perf timing, and a dial9 Tokio flight recorder. What was missing was a live Rust-runtime view: how much CPU/memory the Rust process tree uses right now, how loaded the Tokio runtime is, and which backend operations are slow. ADR-0035 adds exactly that, without an in-process sampling profiler (signal-based samplers like pprof-rs are unavailable/unsafe on Windows) — instead it surfaces the existing dial9 trace files for offline analysis and a live span-hotspot table for attribution. Architecture Layer 1 — Process Tree process.rs samples the current PID plus every descendant. It builds a parent index, computes the descendant set (iterative, cycle-safe), then normalizes CPU and derives disk bytes/sec from the interval. Sidecar detection keys on the bundled Node host: CPU needs two refreshes, so the sampler prime()s a baseline before the first frame. Each ProcessSample carries pid/parentPid/name/role/cpuPct/cpuPctRaw/memBytes/diskReadBps/diskWriteBps/ runSecs. The Processes tab renders a sortable table, a

en.title: Rust Dispatch & OS Bridges
en.text: The native logging half in src-tauri/src/logging — the fern + tauri-plugin-log bootstrap, the Full/Fallback/Disabled mode planner, the PlatformLogger trait with its four backends (Windows Event Log, macOS os log, Linux journald/syslog, noop), the dispatch target round-trip, the log://log webview event, and the six Tauri commands. Rust Dispatch & OS Bridges logging::bootstrap(app) (src-tauri/src/logging/mod.rs:31, called from lib.rs:838) installs tauri-plugin-log with a planned set of targets (stdout + folder + webview) plus a custom fern dispatch target that mirrors every record into the OS logger. A planner (native bootstrap.rs) picks Full (log dir writable), Fallback (dir unavailable → no file target), or Disabled , exposing a NativeLoggingReadiness snapshot to the frontend. The OS bridge is a PlatformLogger trait with four impls — Windows Event Log (source Cognia), macOS os log (subsystem com.cognia.app), Linux journald (syslog fallback), and a noop . The webview target round-trips Rust + sidecar + shell output back to the frontend via the log://log event. Six #[tauri::command]s cover readiness, log-dir access, and the browser→Rust forward. Bootstrap bootstrap() runs unconditionally in the Tauri setup closure (lib.rs:838). It plans the targets, chains the platform dispatch target, and installs the plugin: The global plugin-log level filter is LevelFilter::Info. .targets(...) en.title: Transports
en.text: The nine logging transports, behavior-event exporters, generic OTLP and independent PostHog product/AI destinations, plus the three-state health model. Transports A transport is anything implementing Transport (types/logging/transport.ts:33): a name and a log(entry) method, optionally flush/close/getHealth/getPendingCount. The pipeline fans every redacted entry to all registered transports. Nine implementations exist: console , indexeddb (batched, retention + LRU eviction, cross-tab BroadcastChannel), remote (fetch POST + a durable IndexedDB retry queue + Sentry/Loggly wire shims), native (Tauri invoke to the Rust logger), observability-spool , breadcrumb , otlp-http (exports agent-trace spans), langfuse , and agent-trace (persists embedded spans to Dexie). Product events have a separate structured-envelope exporter fan-out for OTLP Logs and managed/BYO PostHog. Health is exactly healthy degraded offline — there is no unhealthy state. The Transport Interface log() is the only mandatory member. There is no enabled or minLevel field on the interface — enabling is decided in bootstrap.ts, and only native and langfuse expose a per-transport minLevel option (both default "warn"). The health snapshot is a fixed shape (transport.ts:10): console console-transport.ts — one-way synchronous write to globalThis.console, picking the method by level (getConsoleMethod, :122; error+fatal → console.error). Colored %c prefix only in the browser, stack printed separately, traceId truncated to 8 chars. No buffering, no health. name = "console" (:65). indexeddb indexeddb-transport.ts — the durable browser store and the default query source for the log panel . Writes to a dedicated cognia-logs IndexedDB database (separate from the main Dexie DB), object store logs keyed by id with indexes on timestamp/level/module/traceId. Buffered (bufferSize 50, flushInterval 1000 ms). A failed flush re-queues entries via buffer.unshift. remote remote-transport.ts — ships batches to an HTTP endpoint via fetch POST with online/offline awareness, exponential backoff, and a durable IndexedDB retry queue . en.title: Auto-router
en.text: pickDefaultProvider's pure 4-step selection, the per-OS local-engine preference table, how readiness and credential gating actually happen, the connection probe, and the use-case recommendation presets. Auto-router Pure selection — lib/ocr/auto-router.ts When a caller doesn't pin a providerId, pickDefaultProvider(deps) (auto-router.ts:149) chooses one. It is a pure async function — registry, settings, platform, an optional readiness probe, and an optional credentials probe all arrive via AutoRouterDeps, so the whole decision table is unit-testable without a backend. The decision runs four steps: pinned setting → platform-local engine → cloud fallback → last-resort any-enabled. The per-OS preference table is DEFAULT LOCAL PREFERENCE (auto-router.ts:67); MSIX and model-download gating actually happen inside the provider (wired by runtime.ts), not via the router's readiness param in production. The decision ADR-0024 documents three signals (pinned → platform-local → cloud fallback). The code adds a fourth last-resort branch (auto-router.ts:168): it returns any enabled, shell-compatible provider even when cloud fallback is off or uncredentialed, so the router only throws when the registry has nothing shell-compatible at all. Also, the mistral-ocr default is not hardcoded in the router — it comes from settings.cloudFallbackProviderId (whose default lives in DEFAULT OCR SETTINGS). The shared gate isProviderUsable (auto-router.ts:79) is registered && shellAllows && providerEnabled !== false. resolveProviderById (auto-router.ts:182) is the synchronous path used when the caller does pin an id — it throws provider failed for an unknown id and unsupported shell when the provider doesn't run in this shell. The per-OS preference table platformBucket (auto-router.ts:119) merges ...DEFAULT LOCAL PREFERENCE, ...deps.localPreference , then keys by osTag when present, else maps web → browser. Note that the bare tauri / mobile buckets are empty — so the osTag drill-in (windows/macos/linux/ios/android) is required to reach a real local engine on desktop/mobile. local-http is deliberately absent from every bucket (it is user-pinned only). en.title: Overview
en.text: Cross-shell text extraction from images and PDFs — one extract() surface plumbs 20 providers (cloud, LLM-vision, on-device, self-hosted) behind a pure auto-router, a Dexie read-through cache, a two-pass PDF text-layer fast-path, and five native Rust backends. OCR Subsystem Beta · ocrResults schema v36 (DB v70) The OCR subsystem turns an image or PDF into Markdown / plain text / structured blocks through a single entry point — extract(input, deps) (lib/ocr/index.ts:200). Every caller (composer menu, /ocr command, ocr.extract plugin tool) funnels through it, so the SHA-256 read-through cache , the pure auto-router , and the keyring credential lookup all live in one place. Twenty providers register into a shared registry (lib/ocr/runtime.ts:51) spanning four families — cloud document OCR, LLM-vision, on-device engines, and a self-hosted HTTP adapter. PDFs take a text-layer fast-path (lib/ocr/pdf-router.ts:79) that skips OCR on digital pages entirely; five native backends ride opt-in Cargo features in src-tauri/src/ocr/. The OCR subsystem gives every shell — browser (static export), Tauri 2.9 desktop, Capacitor 7 mobile — a first-class way to pull text out of images and PDFs without forwarding them to a multimodal model. The design rationale is in ADR-0024. This section documents the current implementation , module by module — including the handful of places where the code has drifted from the ADR. Where it lives The lifecycle at a glance Each box is a chapter in this section. Read Types & dispatch first — every other module is phrased in terms of OcrInput / OcrResult / OcrProvider. The provider matrix Twenty providers register in ALL PROVIDERS (lib/ocr/runtime.ts:51). en.text: The two-pass PDF router with its text-layer fast-path, the image-prep helpers (normalize, page-range, language, page divider, downscale), the cross-runtime Blob reader, SHA-256 hashing, and the per-provider config parameter schemas. Image normalization, page-range parsing, language normalization, the page divider, and canvas downscaling are pure helpers in image-prep.ts. hash.ts provides the SHA-256 file identity (WebCrypto, not node crypto) that anchors the cache key. ocr-parameter-schemas.ts declares per-provider config forms reusing the main LLM-provider parameter renderer. The pdfjs loader is a DI seam (loadPdf), so tests inject canned pages and the production loader is lazily imported (tree-shaken out of the static export until first use). The per-page decision is the heart of it: defaultPdfLoader (pdf-router.ts:172) dynamically imports pdfjs-dist, and prefers OffscreenCanvas → convertToBlob for rasterization, falling back to a DOM and finally a jsdom-safe base64 path. en.title: Optical Compaction
en.text: Compacting conversation history as an image instead of a summary — the four conservative gates that must all pass, the vision read-back that proves the frame is legible, and the fallback to text that means context is never lost to an unreadable picture. Optical Compaction Experimental · ADR-0063 · opticalArchives (Dexie v101) "Snapcompact" renders the middle of a conversation into a PNG and hands the model the image instead of a text summary, on the bet that a legible rendering carries more of the original than a paraphrase at the same token cost. It is deliberately hard to trigger. compact.mjs runs a four-gate funnel — coverage, budget/overflow, worthwhile, and a round-trip readability check — and any gate that fails returns null, at which point the caller summarizes the very same middle as text. Context is never dropped into an unreadable image. Design rationale: ADR-0063. The readability gate is the whole idea The failure mode of rendering context to an image is silent illegibility: the model receives a picture it cannot read, and the conversation loses the history it thinks it still has. The last gate closes that by round-tripping — the rendered frame is transcribed back through a one-shot vision read (transcribe, the module's only I/O, and injected so the rest is testable offline) and compared against the source. If the read-back does not clear the bar, the frame is discarded and text summarization runs instead. The three earlier gates are cheaper filters: is enough of the middle actually covered, does the render fit the budget without overflowing, and is the result worth the substitution at all. Where it lives Fonts are embedded (fonts-data.mjs) rather than resolved from the system, so a frame renders identically regardless of what the host machine has installed — a rendering that varies by machine would make the readability gate non-reproducible. Persistence is a deliberate side effect lib/claude/optical-archive-persist.ts bridges the sidecar's compact boundary event to the Dexie store, and it is kept out of the pure adapter.ts reducer on purpose — it is a best-effort, browser-only side effect, mirroring how pre messages routes to the in-memory undo registry. The Dexie module is imported dynamically so adapter.ts keeps no DB dependency and stays safe to import under SSR and in tests. The table itself is small: opticalArchives: "&id, sessionId, created

en.title: Performance diagnostics
en.text: Versioned Renderer and selected-host metrics, demand leases, encrypted captures, portable evidence, and comparison rules. Source and surface contract The performance subsystem never treats “running Cognia” as one process or one clock. A full authenticated shell registers its local Renderer document source; lightweight, transparent, pairing, OAuth and overlay routes do not. The selected execution target may independently advertise a Rust/Tauri or Node/headless host source. Renderer and host data are never merged into one synthetic series. Surface Renderer Captures Selected host Host controls --- --- --- --- --- Web full shell available, including offline available while account is unlocked only when paired target advertises it only advertised actions with a valid remote grant Capacitor full shell available, including offline available while account is unlocked only when paired target advertises it same host-owned challenge flow Tauri full WebView one independent source per document available local Rust source local owner routing; folder reveal is local-only Node/headless host not applicable to the host process host capture lease process, heap, event-loop, RPC and managed workers unsupported actions are omitted Lightweight/transparent route excluded an existing capture continues in the shell owner excluded excluded Every capability resolves to connecting, live, stale, error or unsupported. A collection failure and a missing capability are explicit and are never projected as zero. Demand lifecycle PerfLease replaces panel-owned start/stop state. Open is bound to device, target and routing generation, purpose and requested cadence. Renew runs every five seconds and remote expiry is 15 seconds. A normal unmount closes immediately. The host admits one live and one capture lease per device, 16 per host and no cadence faster than 500 ms. One physical sampler runs at the fastest admitted cadence and dispatches/down-samples independently per lease. Listeners attach before open and snapshot. Frames merge only when target, routing generation, host incarnation, sampling session and sequence match. Recoverable gaps trigger snapshot refill; unrecoverable gaps remain visible and are persisted with captures. Runtime rates use actual monotonic elapsed time and reset whenever cadence, source incarnation, boot/process/runtime session, sleep, clock or counter continuity changes.

en.title: Adapter Model & Registry

One interface, eleven builders, two parallel registries. Adapter Model & Registry Every platform connector implements the single PlatformAdapter interface (types/connectors/adapter.ts:135): lifecycle (start/stop/health), one non-optional mutation (send), a fan of optional mutations (streamReply?/edit?/delete?/setTyping?/uploadFile?/fetchHistory?), and the required synchronous a2uiCapability() (types/connectors/adapter.ts:180) read on the hot send path by build-options. The runtime factory buildAdapterFromRow(row) (lib/connectors/adapter-registry.ts:42) switches on row.type across 11 builders, each probing its self-id and wiring lazy credential resolvers (rotation-safe). A parallel pure display registry CONNECTOR METADATA (lib/connectors/adapter-metadata.ts:42, 16 rows) feeds the Discover page — its status now mirrors native adapter availability while retaining planned rows for reserved kinds. The PlatformAdapter Contract Every connector — built-in or plugin-contributed — implements interface PlatformAdapter (types/connectors/adapter.ts:135). The contract is deliberately minimal: a stable meta/id, a three-method lifecycle, exactly one non-optional mutation (send), and a required synchronous capability probe. Everything else is optional and feature-detected at the call site. en.title: Auto-mode AI Loop & A2UI Bridge
en.text: The non-stub auto-mode turn — safeSendPrompt gating raw IM text on the same PII red-line the chat composer never has to enforce — plus the bidirectional A2UI bridge that projects assistant replies into platform-native rich content, lifts inbound rich content back into surfaces, mints round-trippable callback ids, and the execution bridge + run-presentation runner that project workflow / team runs into per-conversation run cards. Auto-mode AI Loop & A2UI Bridge When an inbound IM message drives a Claude turn with no human in the loop, the connector subsystem cannot reuse the reviewed chat composer path — so safeSendPrompt (lib/connectors/ai-loop/safe-send-prompt.ts:69) wraps runAndCaptureAssistantReply with the same PII red-line lib/twin/ingest/ enforces: walk the prompt and the build-options appendSystemPrompt, call hasNoLeakingPii on each, and abort before the model (writing a pii blocked audit row) rather than redact — there is no human to decide what to drop. The captured reply is projected to transferable segments by assistantReplyToSegments (a2ui-to-segments.ts:52), inbound platform-rich content is projected into an InboundA2UIBlock by projectInboundToA2UI (inbound-a2ui-dispatch.ts:26) for the Inbox renderer, plugins author surfaces declaratively via createA2UIBuilder (surface-builder.ts:315), the build-options resolver appends a capability-aware downgrade section (buildCapabilityPromptSection, capability-evaluator.ts:30), interactive components round-trip through buildActionId / recordCallbackBinding / resolveCallbackBinding ( shared/a2ui-mapper.ts), and workflow / team runs reach IM as durable run cards via startWorkflowExecutionBridge (lib/execution/workflow-bridge.ts:143) + startExecutionRunPresentationRunner (lib/connectors/run-presentation/runner.ts:715). This page is the middle of the connector pipeline. The ConnectorBus decides whether to reply; this layer decides what to say and how to shape it for the channel; everything terminates by calling enqueueOutbound and handing off to the Outbound Queue. The A2UI vocabulary itself lives in A2UI; workflow runs that trigger from IM are covered by Visual Workflows. See the subsystem overview for where this sits in the larger stack. en.title: Built-in Adapters
en.text: The eleven in-tree IM platform adapters — Telegram, Discord, Lark, OneBot, Slack, QQ-Official, WeCom, WeChat-OA, WeChat-Personal, DingTalk, and Matrix. Each is a parse + serialize + transport + capability bundle assembled by a createXxxAdapter factory; inbound flows adapter → gate → emit → bus, interactive callbacks bypass emit and call dispatchConnectorCallback. Built-in Adapters Eleven built-in adapters ship in-tree under lib/connectors/adapters/ /. Each follows the same decomposition — parse.ts (platform envelope → NormalizedInboundEvent), serialize.ts (OutboundRequest → platform call), one or more transport- .ts drivers, a capability.ts matrix, and an index.ts createXxxAdapter(opts) factory that wires them together. Inbound takes a single path: the transport yields raw frames, the parser normalises them, gateInboundEvent (lib/connectors/at-gate.ts) applies the at-strategy + allow/blocklist gate, then ctx.emit(event) lands on bus.dispatchInboundFull. Interactive callbacks bypass emit — inline buttons / cards / interactions call getBus().dispatchConnectorCallback(...) directly so the A2UI surface binding is recovered. Transports span long-poll, webhook, gateway (WSS), reverse-WS, Socket Mode, Stream Mode, and Matrix /sync. The eleven adapters are the concrete implementations of the PlatformAdapter contract. This page covers what is common to all of them, the full transport/signature matrix, and a deep dive into the four reference adapters. The Rust signaling/decrypt plane they lean on is documented in the Rust layer; how inbound events are gated is in inbound gating; how each adapter advertises rich content is in AI & A2UI. Common Decomposition Every adapter directory is the same shape, so once you know one you know all eleven: File Responsibility --- --- parse.ts Platform event envelope → NormalizedInboundEvent (sender, channel, mentions, segments). serialize.ts OutboundRequest → platform API call(s) (text, media, reactions, edits). transport- .ts The connection driver (long-poll loop, gateway WS client, webhook subscriber, …). capability.ts The static capability flags + A2UI capability matrix for this platform. index.ts The createXxxAdapter(opts) factory that assembles all of the above into a PlatformAdapter. en.title: ConnectorBus & Runtime
en.text: The singleton fan-in/fan-out hub for Platform Connectors — its 11-step inbound pipeline, interactive callback dispatch, workflow fan-out, the AI-run runtime, and credential hot-reload. ConnectorBus & Runtime ConnectorBus is the single in-process hub every platform adapter fans into. One method — dispatchInboundFull (lib/connectors/bus.ts:208) — drives the ordered 11-step inbound pipeline (dedup → adapter lookup → binding → policy → route → fan-out). A parallel method, dispatchConnectorCallback (lib/connectors/bus.ts:721), handles interactive button/select/form events with five kind-specific short-circuits. The runtime (lib/connectors/runtime.ts:288) installs bus.routeHandler to turn an ai-run decision into a captured Claude turn enqueued for outbound delivery. Lifecycle (lib/connectors/lifecycle.ts) tracks running adapters and hot-reloads them on credential rotation. The ConnectorBus is the single owner of the routing decision for every inbound platform event. Adapters never decide whether to reply — they normalize a platform payload into a NormalizedInboundEvent and hand it to the bus. Everything downstream (dedup, character binding, policy gate, AI turn, workflow fan-out) is the bus's responsibility. See the subsystem overview for where the bus sits in the larger connector stack, and adapter model for what an adapter contributes. The Singleton ConnectorBus is a class (lib/connectors/bus.ts:78) reached through a lazy singleton getBus() (lib/connectors/bus.ts:1079). Adapters register on start and unregister on stop: Two passive observer channels let plugins tap traffic without owning the decision. subscribeInbound (lib/connectors/bus.ts:137) feeds every inbound event to ctx.connectors.onInbound before routing; subscribeCallback (lib/connectors/bus.ts:162) feeds every resolved interactive callback to ctx.connectors.onCallback. Both are strictly read-only — a throwing observer is swallowed and never alters routing (lib/connectors/bus.ts:144, lib/connectors/bus.ts:171). The authoritative seams are two nullable fields: routeHandler (lib/connectors/bus.ts:103, installed by the runtime) and callbackHandler (lib/connectors/bus.ts:111, wired to the A2UI bridge). en.title: Cross-shell relay
en.text: How an Inbox write executes on a phone, a browser, or a desktop driving a remote host — one shell-agnostic facade, one idempotency key, and two realtime signals. Cross-shell relay The Inbox used to work fully only on the machine running the adapters. Every reply surface decided for itself how to write, and only the desktop's decision worked: a phone's approval flipped a draft without ever enqueuing delivery, a browser rendered controls that did nothing, and a desktop driving a remote host wrote to the wrong database. ADR-0131 replaces those twelve decisions with one seam. Components describe the write; lib/connectors/inbox-writes/ decides where it runs. The four writes No caller branches on isTauri() or the platform. resolveInboxWriteRoute() (lib/connectors/inbox-writes/route.ts:77) resolves one of three routes: Route When Executes --------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- "remote" this desktop drives a remote host (isRemoteHostActive()) mobileOutboundQueue → RPC on the paired host "local" this shell owns a connector runtime local.ts, against this process's Dexie + delivery gateway "remote" a companion target is active (paired phone, web companion) durable queue → RPC "unavailable" standalone browser / unpaired phone throws InboxWriteUnavailableError Order matters. A desktop driving a remote host still advertises connector-runtime from its capability baseline, but its local runtime is torn down while the remote is active. If "local" won, the reply would become an outbound job no running adapter would ever deliver. One implementation, two callers lib/connectors/inbox-writes/local.ts holds the three primitives — sendManualReplyLocally, approveDraftLocally, rejectDraftLocally — lifted verbatim out of components/chat/composer.tsx. The host RPC arms call the same functions . lib/companion/desktop-write-source.ts dispatches connector enqueue outbound / connector approve draft / connector reject draft straight into local.ts, so a phone-originated reply and a desktop-originated reply produce byte-identical outboundQueue and messages rows. There is no second implementation to drift. Idempotency is end to end The client mints one crypto.randomUUID() per write and threads it through every layer: 1. the mobileOutboundQueue row's idempotencyKey; 2. the Idempotency-Key head

en.title: Health, Audit & Help
en.text: Two-tier adapter liveness, the capped audit ring, the 24h health-history derivation, and the cross-provider help/welcome dispatch for the Platform Connectors subsystem. Health, Audit & Help Every running adapter is probed by a single bus-scope heartbeat sweep : an active adapter.health() snapshot every 30 s, plus a passive liveness probe every 2nd tick for transports that sit idle (Lark webhook, OneBot reverse-WS). Heartbeats land in a dedicated connectorHeartbeats table; real events land in a 5000-row capped connectorAudit ring spanning a 48-kind vocabulary . A pure deriveHistory folds both into the Health Tab's 24h × 30 min dot grid. The same audit ring records the cross-provider help / welcome dispatch, which short-circuits the AI turn when a user types /help. This page covers the observability and self-description plane of the connector runtime. For the dispatch core see Connector Bus, for send mechanics see Outbound Queue, for the rich-card builder see AI & A2UI, and for the axum transports see Rust Layer. Two-tier Liveness Adapters fall into two transport classes. Active transports drive an explicit health signal — a Telegram long-poll loop, a Discord Gateway socket, Slack Socket Mode — so when the transport detaches, adapter.health() flips to degraded on its own. Passive transports (Lark webhook, OneBot reverse-WS) sit idle waiting for the platform or client to push events; from the adapter's point of view "no events for an hour" and "we're fine, traffic is quiet" look identical (passive-heartbeat.ts:10-13). The two are distinguished by a single predicate: Since schema v51 a single bus-scope interval (heartbeat-sweep.ts) services every running adapter per tick, replacing the old per-adapter timer fan-out (up to 2N timers). It reuses recordHeartbeatNow / recordPassiveProbe verbatim, so the rows written are identical — only the scheduling is consolidated. The Nth-tick cadence is derived from the two intervals so the relationship stays explicit: The first tick fires immediately so the Health view has data without waiting a full interval (heartbeat-sweep.ts:139), and sweepRunning skips the next scheduler fire rather than piling a second concurrent sweep on top of a slow one (heartbeat-sweep.ts:97, 129-137). Active Heartbeat recordHeartbeatNow(adapter, options?) takes one snapshot now — exported so the Health Tab's Reconnect-now button and integration test

en.title: Inbound Gating & Policy
en.text: How the Platform Connectors subsystem decides which inbound messages reach the AI — the cross-platform @-gate, the dedup ledger, TriggerPolicy evaluation, three-layer binding resolution, and the mode router. Inbound Gating & Policy Every inbound platform message runs a gauntlet before it can reach ctx.emit() and the AI. First a dedup ledger drops replays. Then a per-adapter @-gate (shouldRespondToMessage) applies blocklist / allowlist / at-strategy guardrails. Surviving events hit the bus, which resolves a three-layer binding (adapter → character → conversation override) into a (mode, characterId, trigger) triple, runs the pure evaluatePolicy evaluator (OR-ed rules, first-match blockers), and feeds the result to the mode router which picks one of five RouteDecisions — ai-run, manual-store, draft-prepare, store-only, or drop. Two-stage gating Inbound gating is intentionally split into two stages that run at different points in the pipeline: 1. Adapter-side @-gate — runs inside each adapter dispatcher, immediately before ctx.emit(). It is platform-agnostic (lib/connectors/at-gate.ts, schema v45) and answers a coarse question: should the bot even acknowledge this chat / message at all? It reads operator-configured fields off the AdapterInstanceRow (chat blocklist / allowlist, at-strategy) and short-circuits before the event ever crosses into the bus. 2. Bus-side policy — once an event is emitted, the bus resolves the binding and runs the fine-grained TriggerPolicy (lib/connectors/policy-eval.ts) to decide how to respond: AI-run now, store for a human, or prepare a draft. Before either stage, the dedup ledger (lib/connectors/dedup.ts) guarantees a given platform message is processed exactly once. Dedup Ledger recordAndCheckInbound is the idempotency guard. It records (adapterId, namespace, platformMessageId) and returns true only the first time that tuple is seen, so retried webhooks, reconnect replays, and duplicate callback deliveries are dropped cheaply. Namespace (InboundLedgerNamespace) defaults to "inbound" (dedup.ts:35) for back-compat with every pre-v38 caller. Callback handlers pass "callback"; first-contact greeters pass "welcome". Each namespace is an independent sliding window, so a message id can recur across buckets without colliding. Lazy prune — PRUNE EVERY = 200 (dedup.ts:16) and LEDGER CAP = 10 000 (dedup.ts:17). Every 200th call awaits pruneOl

en.title: Platform Connectors
en.text: Turn AI characters into real bots on 11 IM platforms — a singleton ConnectorBus fan-in/out, a three-layer binding stack, a Dexie-backed FIFO outbound queue with circuit breaker + token bucket + dead-letter, a PII-gated auto-mode AI loop, and a bidirectional A2UI rich-content bridge. Webhook signature verification and long-lived sockets live in Rust. Platform Connectors Eleven built-in IM adapters (Telegram · Discord · Slack · Lark · OneBot v11/v12 · WeCom · WeChat OA · personal WeChat · QQ official · DingTalk · Matrix) fan in to a singleton ConnectorBus (lib/connectors/bus.ts:78). Every inbound message runs an 11-step pipeline — dedup → adapter lookup → three-layer binding resolve → TriggerPolicy evaluate → mode route → audit → help/welcome → route handler → workflow fan-out. Outbound goes through a Dexie FIFO queue (lib/connectors/outbound-runner.ts:284) wrapped in a per-conversation lane, circuit breaker, token bucket, exponential backoff, idempotency LRU, and a dead-letter sink. Three modes — auto (PII-gated AI reply), manual (human typed), draft (AI drafts, human approves). Webhook signature verification (HMAC / Ed25519 / AES-CBC) and the OneBot / Discord / Lark sockets run in Rust (src-tauri/src/connectors/). Rich interactive content is projected through the A2UI bridge both directions, with callback bindings persisted in Dexie. What It Is Platform Connectors turns any Cognia character into a real bot on real IM platforms. An operator configures an adapter in Settings → Connections , binds it to a character, and the bot answers — in auto mode it runs a full Claude turn through the same build-options pipeline as the in-app chat; in draft mode the AI prepares a reply a human approves from the Inbox; in manual mode a human types through the bot. The subsystem is a clean fan-in / fan-out around one singleton: Fan-in — each adapter normalizes its platform payload into a NormalizedInboundEvent and calls bus.dispatchInboundFull(event). The bus dedups, resolves the binding, evaluates the trigger policy, routes by mode, and hands off to the runtime. Fan-out — outbound replies (AI / manual / draft-approved / workflow) are enqueued into a single Dexie queue and drained by one pump that applies quiet-hours, mute, circuit breaking, rate limiting, backoff, and dead-lettering — uniformly, regardless of source.
