en.title: Outbound Queue & Delivery
en.text: The durable outboundQueue, the event-driven pump, and the per-adapter delivery gauntlet — circuit breaker, token bucket, exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency LRU, per-conversation FIFO lanes, dead-lettering, and the scheduled / housekeeping surfaces that feed and prune it. Outbound Queue & Delivery Every reply the assistant sends to a platform is a durable row in the Dexie outboundQueue table, not a direct adapter call. A single wake-driven loop — startOutboundRunner (lib/connectors/outbound-runner.ts:284) — drains due rows into per-conversation FIFO lanes and runs each job through an ordered gauntlet: re-fetch → muted → quiet-hours → idempotency → circuit breaker → token bucket → max-attempts → dispatch (processJob, lib/connectors/outbound-runner.ts:345). Failures retry with exponential backoff + jitter up to MAX ATTEMPTS=5, then dead-letter. The loop never busy-polls: it sleeps until the next retry deadline (peekNextWakeAt) or a fresh enqueue wake (subscribeOutboundEnqueued, lib/db/outbound-jobs.ts:64). Two scheduler executors (lib/connectors/scheduled-outbound.ts:375) feed the queue — one direct, one a full AI turn — and three housekeeping sweeps prune callback bindings, age the queue at its soft cap, and export the dead-letter queue. =5 events in 30s window" / Outbound delivery is the back half of the connector pipeline. The ConnectorBus decides whether to reply and AI & A2UI decides what to say; both terminate by calling enqueueOutbound. From that point the runner owns reliability — ordering, retries, rate limiting, and the circuit breaker — so no inbound path or workflow node ever blocks on a slow or failing platform API. See the subsystem overview for where this sits in the larger stack. The Queue outboundQueue is a Dexie table (lib/db/outbound-jobs.ts) whose rows move through a five-state lifecycle. OutboundJobStatus is "pending" "sending" "sent" "failed" "deadlettered"; OutboundJobSource records provenance as "ai-run" "manual" "workflow" "draft-approved" so the inbox UI can badge each row and the audit log can drill down on origin. Every enqueue funnels through one chokepoint: The request body is an OutboundRequest (types/connectors/outbound.ts:4): conversationRef, segments, optional replyTo / threadId / editTargetMessageId (types/connectors/outbound.ts:17), and a metadata object whose idempotencyKey is required (types/connectors/outbound.ts

en.title: Rust Layer
en.text: The native Tauri backend of the Platform Connectors subsystem — an axum webhook receiver with per-platform signature verification, OS-keyring credential custody, a OneBot reverse-WS bridge, a generic outbound WS client, the Feishu protobuf long-connection, a rate-limited HTTP client, media upload, and an AES-256-GCM attachment cache, exposed to the renderer through 21 Tauri commands and four event-channel families. Rust Layer Anything a connector needs that a static-export renderer cannot do safely lives in src-tauri/src/connectors/: inbound HTTP webhook reception with constant-time signature verification (sigverify/ ), long-lived WebSocket sockets (OneBot reverse-WS in ws server.rs, generic outbound in ws client.rs, Feishu protobuf long-conn in lark ws.rs), OS-keyring secret custody (keyring.rs), a per-host rate-limited HTTP client (http client.rs), and an AES-256-GCM on-disk attachment cache (attachments.rs). The axum router (axum app.rs) dispatches each POST /webhook/ type / id by the registered adapter type — never the URL segment — so a spoofed path cannot skip verification, then emits the parsed (and for Lark, decrypted) body on connectors://webhook/ . All of it is reachable from the TS side through 21 #[tauri::command]s (commands.rs) registered in lib.rs, and surfaces inbound traffic on four Tauri event-channel families. This is the native floor under the TS adapter model and the eleven built-in adapters: the adapters call typed wrappers in lib/connectors/tauri/commands.ts, which invoke the Rust commands below. Inbound frames the Rust layer emits are consumed by the transports and fed through inbound gating; how each adapter advertises rich content is in AI & A2UI. Why Rust Three classes of work are forced down into native code: Signature verification must run where the raw request body and the secret meet without crossing the IPC boundary or living in a JS heap. Each platform's scheme — Telegram's secret-token header, Slack's HMAC-SHA256 basestring, Discord's Ed25519, Lark's token + AES decrypt, WeChat's SHA-1 + AES — is implemented in sigverify/ .rs with subtle::ConstantTimeEq comparisons so a wrong signature leaks no timing. Long-lived sockets — OneBot's reverse-WS server, Discord/Slack outbound gateways, and Feishu's binary protobuf long-connection — need a persistent native event loop. en.title: Inbox UI & Plugin Extension
en.text: The ConnectorBusProvider bootstrap spine, the responsive three-pane Inbox shell, the seven-tab Connections settings, the live Dexie bindings, and the plugin adapter extension contract. Inbox UI & Plugin Extension The Platform Connectors UI is anchored by a single Tauri-only React provider — ConnectorBusProvider — whose one useEffect runs a strict twelve-step bootstrap that boots the bus singleton, wires the runtime + callback handler, registers and starts every enabled adapter, and launches four background runners. Everything the operator sees (the three-pane Inbox shell, the seven-tab Connections settings, mode switcher, draft editor, outbound pill) is a thin reactive view over Dexie tables via useLiveQuery. Plugins extend the fleet by declaring connectors in their manifest; registerPluginAdapters builds each factory's adapter and hands it to the same bus — no new transport, no privileged path. The Bootstrap Spine: ConnectorBusProvider ConnectorBusProvider( children ) (components/connectors/connector-bus-provider.tsx:54) is the spine of the whole subsystem. It renders nothing but < children — all behaviour lives in one useEffect that fires once on mount. The provider is a strict no-op in web mode: if (!isTauri()) return (connector-bus-provider.tsx:56) bails before any work, because every connector transport (axum, keyring) is a Rust shim that only exists in the Tauri shell. The bootstrap is an ordered twelve-step sequence : 1. Tauri guard — if (!isTauri()) return (connector-bus-provider.tsx:56). 2. Teardown state — allocate the AbortController, cancelled flag, and startedAdapters array the cleanup closure later reads (connector-bus-provider.tsx:58-63). 3. List enabled rows — listEnabledAdapterInstances() inside a try/catch that swallows a NotFoundError (stale IndexedDB schema) instead of crashing the app (connector-bus-provider.tsx:148-167). 4. Acquire the bus — const bus = getBus() returns the process singleton (connector-bus-provider.tsx:170). 5. Install the runtime — installRuntime(bus, runAndCapture: runAndCaptureAssistantReply ) wires the ai-run branch to a real Claude turn (connector-bus-provider.tsx:177). 6. Wire the callback handler — bus.callbackHandler = defaultConnectorCallbackHandler so inbound interactive events project onto the matching A2UI surface (connector-bus-provider.tsx:183). 7. en.title: Agent SDK (ctx.agent)
en.text: The embeddable agent runtime exposed to plugins — typed run / runStreamed with structured output, rewrite-capable tool permission gates, and invokeTool for reusing host tools by name. Agent SDK (ctx.agent) ctx.agent is the embeddable counterpart to the chat agent. Beyond the registration methods (registerTool / registerSkill / registerSubagent / …) it now exposes a typed run loop: run(prompt, options) (one-shot) and runStreamed(prompt, options) (an async-iterable of typed events). Both wrap lib/ai/agent/agent-executor.ts:executeAgent — text-only by default, tool-enabled through the desktop sidecar when toolsEnabled is set (gated by the agent:control permission). Runs support structured JSON output (outputFormat), a rewrite-capable canUseTool permission gate, and invokeTool(name, args) for calling any host/plugin tool by name. The legacy executeAgent(config) is kept as a deprecated shim. Why it exists Plugins could already register tools and subagents, but the only way to run an agentic turn was the untyped ctx.agent.executeAgent(config: Record ). There was no typed contract, no streaming to the plugin, no structured output, no way to gate or rewrite tool-call arguments, and no way to invoke a host tool from inside plugin code. The Agent SDK closes those gaps, borrowing the embeddable-agent shape from the VS Code Language Model API, the Anthropic Claude Agent SDK (query()), the Cursor SDK, and the OpenAI Agents SDK. run — one-shot run resolves with a PluginAgentRunResult. en.title: Core runtime
en.text: The PluginManager lifecycle engine in lib/plugin/core/ — a per-shell lazy singleton that discovers, validates, compat-gates, signature-verifies, loads, activates, and enables every plugin, with snapshot rollback at each step, plus the loader, contribution registry, descriptor builder, transport gateway, and dependency topo-sort. Core runtime The core runtime (lib/plugin/core/) is the lifecycle engine of the plugin platform. Its center is PluginManager (manager.ts:364), a lazy per-shell singleton (getPluginManager manager.ts:317, initializePluginManager manager.ts:336) configured by resolvePluginRuntimeBootstrap (bootstrap.ts:21), which picks the browser-vs-Tauri profile and refuses to run in a non-main window. The manager wires four collaborators in its constructor (manager.ts:381) — PluginLoader, PluginRegistry, a PluginLifecycleHooks manager, and lazy A2UI/Themes bridges — then walks each plugin through a status machine installed → loaded → enabled → disabled → uninstalled . Discovery (scanPlugins manager.ts:873) validates, compat- checks, and signature-checks every manifest before writing to the Zustand usePluginStore; enablePlugin (manager.ts:1524) gates dependencies, applies Dexie tables + i18n, and registers contributions; every reverse path captures a rollback snapshot. What It Is lib/plugin/core/ is where a plugin becomes alive . Everything else in the plugin platform — the ctx. API, the contribution bridges, the security guard, the marketplace — hangs off the lifecycle that PluginManager drives. The manager is the single owner of plugin state transitions: it is the only code that calls a plugin's activate(context), registers its contributions, applies its Dexie tables, and tears it all back down on disable or uninstall. The runtime is shell-aware. resolvePluginRuntimeBootstrap (bootstrap.ts:21) inspects the host — browser, Tauri desktop, or a secondary window — and produces a PluginManagerConfig. A non-main window is refused outright, so only one manager instance ever drives discovery and loading. en.title: Plugin system
en.text: Cognia's first-party plugin runtime — a lazy-loaded PluginManager that discovers, validates, signs, loads, and activates plugins; a 48-namespace permission-gated context API; 34 contribution bridge files into host subsystems; a declarative contracts/registries/SDK layer; per-call consent + Ed25519 signing; WASM and VS Code-extension runtimes; and a four-source marketplace with backup/rollback lifecycle. Plugin system A plugin in Cognia is a signed, manifest-described bundle that the host loads into an isolated runtime and grants a capability-scoped API (ctx). The central orchestrator is PluginManager (lib/plugin/core/manager.ts:364) — a lazy singleton that walks every plugin through discover → validate → compat-gate → verify-signature → load → activate → enable → register-contributions, with snapshot-based rollback at every step. Plugins extend the app three ways: by calling the ctx. API (≈48 permission-gated namespaces assembled in lib/plugin/core/context.ts:233), by declaring contributions that 34 bridge files (lib/plugin/bridge/) project into host subsystems (chat, themes, fonts, Monaco, connectors, workflows, scheduler…), and by registering typed items into overlay registries via define () SDK helpers. Every host-touching call passes through createGuardedAPI (lib/plugin/security/permission-guard.ts:777): explicit-grant check, per-call consent for dangerous permissions, and a token-bucket rate limiter. JS runs in a new Function sandbox; WASM runs in a Rust wasmtime host; full VS Code extensions run through a sidecar shim. What It Is Cognia ships a real plugin platform, not a script hook. Third-party (and first-party in-tree) code extends the app without forking it, under explicit per-permission user consent. A plugin can: Call host capabilities through ctx. — chat, vector search, the agent, the filesystem, the terminal, git, connectors, computer-use automation, the companion device, and more. Contribute surfaces declared in its manifest — themes, fonts, wallpapers, icon themes, TextMate grammars, languages, snippets, message-part renderers, A2UI components, config panels, modal mounts, AI/OCR/workspace providers, connector adapters, chat middlewares. en.title: Pro IDE
en.text: code-server embedded as a real editor pane — a loopback TCP control channel to a companion VS Code extension so agents can apply undo-able edits, plus the theme and locale plumbing that makes the embedded workbench actually look and speak like the app. Pro IDE Beta · ADR-0088 · disk + settings.json (no Dexie) The Pro IDE is a real code-server instance in a webview, driven by the app. Opening a file is easy — code-server's own CLI does --reuse-window : : . Everything past that is not: the CLI can only open and reveal, so an undo-able edit or a read of the active editor has to run inside the VS Code extension host. That is what the companion extension (sidecar/codeserver-agent-ext/) and the loopback control channel (src-tauri/src/codeserver/agent channel.rs) exist for. The managed channel is JSON-RPC 2.0 with Content-Length framing over a TCP socket on 127.0.0.1, not a WebSocket . The old newline bridge is compatibility-only for one release. See the Managed IDE Extension Platform for profiles, proxy signing, capability negotiation, content handles, and the public author contract. Design rationale: ADR-0088. Why a dedicated channel, and why TCP Both ends of this channel are ours, and neither crosses a proxy or a browser. WebSocket's handshake, framing and client-side masking would be pure ceremony, so protocol 1.0 uses JSON-RPC 2.0 with LSP-style Content-Length framing over loopback TCP. A challenge/HMAC handshake authenticates the session before the connection is published. The legacy newline parser exposes only the original editor-control methods. Its hosting is the more interesting decision. It lives in the codeserver module, not in the opt-in companion api server, so it comes up and tears down with the code-server processes it drives. A user who has never enabled remote access still gets a fully working editor — the agent↔IDE path is not gated behind a remote-access toggle it has nothing to do with. Where it lives open-file-queue.ts exists because open requests can arrive before the instance is up; queueing them is what stops an early "open file" from being silently dropped. Composer integration Trigger detection components/chat/composer-trigger.ts already had a namespace mechanism for @skill: and @preset:. The document providers join it, with one difference: every other namespaced kind maps 1:1 to a TriggerKind, whereas all providers share the single kind "doc" and are told apart by which prefix the user typed. The prefix list is read from the registry on every call rather than snapshotted at module load, so a test that resets the registry does not leave it stale: Namespaced prefixes are mode-dependent. The team workspace (mentionMode="agents") reserves @ for members and gets no typed prefixes; the workflow editor gets @node: / @edge: instead. Panel state hooks/chat/use-remote-doc-search.ts owns three things the popover's other branches do not: an account list, a pure link-recognition fast path, and a provider that may not implement search at all. Two ways to reach a document, in priority order: 1. The typed query is itself a link or token. matchRef resolves it synchronously — no network, and no account needed to see the row. 2. Otherwise, keyword search through the connected account, debounced 250 ms, capped at 20 hits, and sequence-guarded so a slow response cannot overwrite a newer one. composer-popover.tsx lists this hook's result in a useMemo dependency array. A fresh object identity on every render would invalidate the whole candidate list each frame and reset the keyboard highlight while the user is still typing. The account list is reloaded whenever the panel opens for a different provider and is deliberately not cached across opens: connecting an account in Settings while the composer is mounted must be visible on the next @ without a reload. The footer strip shows the active account — as plain text for a single account, as a Select when several are bound (with mousedown stopped so choosing one does not blur the textarea and dismiss the popover). en.text: Docs and Sheets on a read-only Workspace connection — why the device-code flow cannot work, and how the installed-app loopback redirect lands on the Rust connectors server. Google provider lib/docs-providers/providers/google/ · prefix @gdoc: · kinds doc, sheet Why the device-code flow cannot be reused The repository already had one Google OAuth implementation: the Drive backup destination (lib/data/destinations/google-oauth.ts), which uses the device-code flow because it needs no redirect listener and therefore runs unchanged on the headless brain. That flow cannot serve this feature. Google restricts "OAuth 2.0 for TV and Limited-Input Devices" to a fixed scope list: email, openid, profile, drive.appdata, drive.file and the YouTube scopes. None of the read scopes required here is on it, so a device-code connection physically cannot read a document the user already owns — drive.file sees only files this app created. Sharing a keyring key would couple them: reconnecting one would break the other's identity, and widening the backup connection's drive.file scope would hand a write-only-to-its-own-folder integration a read of the user's entire Drive. They live under different keyring namespaces and may be different Google accounts. Scopes and storage All three are needed: drive.readonly lists and searches files and exports a Doc, but cannot read a multi-worksheet spreadsheet; spreadsheets.readonly supplies per-worksheet values; documents.readonly backs the structured Docs read. en.title: Overview
en.text: Reference Feishu and Google Workspace documents from the chat composer with @lark: and @gdoc: — a provider registry sibling to Platform Connectors, delivering bodies through the existing attachment pipeline rather than a second one. Remote Documents Beta · desktop only · no Dexie schema The composer's @ could only reference files with a local path. Remote Documents adds a peer registry — lib/docs-providers/ — whose providers answer three questions about documents that live in a third-party cloud: is this pasted string mine (matchRef), what matches these keywords (search), and give me the body as text (fetch). Picking one in the @lark: / @gdoc: panel fetches it immediately and stages it as a synthesized File, which rejoins the ordinary attachment pipeline. Two providers ship: Feishu (docs, wiki nodes, spreadsheets, Bitable) borrowing a bound Lark connector's credentials, and Google Workspace (Docs, Sheets) on its own read-only OAuth connection. Both are desktop-only for concrete transport reasons. Decision record: ADR-0134. Why it is not part of Platform Connectors ADR-0009 confines PlatformAdapter to IM conversation semantics — send, edit, reactions, chat management, an A2UI capability matrix. Adding searchDocuments() there would force Google to be modelled as a connector with no messaging, whose send, health and a2uiCapability are empty stubs. So lib/docs-providers/ is a sibling registry, not an extension. The Feishu provider still uses a connector instance's credentials, because that is where the user's Feishu account already lives — borrowing beats a second connection the user would have to authorize and revoke separately. The whole path What each provider covers Provider Prefix Kinds Credentials Search --- --- --- --- --- Feishu / Lark @lark: doc, wiki, sheet, bitable a bound Lark connector instance yes (user identity required) Google Workspace @gdoc: doc, sheet its own read-only OAuth connection yes (Drive files.list) Slides and mindnotes are excluded on both sides: neither platform offers a useful public text read, so the picker never offers something that can only fail at fetch time. Delivery: fetch on pick, send as an attachment A picked document is fetched immediately and staged as a synthesized File, which rejoins the pipeline every dropped or pasted document already uses: This is the decision that keeps the feature small. en.title: Feishu provider
en.text: Docs, wiki nodes, spreadsheets and Bitable through a bound Lark connector's credentials, on one extracted authentication harness. Feishu provider lib/docs-providers/providers/lark/ · prefix @lark: · kinds doc, wiki, sheet, bitable Credentials are borrowed, never new listAccounts() projects the enabled Lark adapter rows — the same list components/twin/lark-account-picker.tsx shows — and labels each with the connected OAuth user when there is one: The account id is the adapter id, so a fetch runs against exactly the tenant the user picked. Nothing here reads the keyring — that happens inside the auth harness. One authentication harness lib/twin/ingest/lark-doc-fetcher.ts owned the only implementation of "resolve the best Lark identity, refresh silently, fall back to the bot". Rather than copy it for spreadsheets and Bitable, it was extracted to lib/connectors/adapters/lark/authed-api.ts and the fetcher rewritten onto it. Its existing 41 tests pin that the behaviour did not move. The harness, in order: 1. refuses off Tauri unless a transport is injected (LarkAccessError("browserUnsupported")); 2. loads the adapter row, then appId / appSecret from the connectors keyring; 3. prefers the OAuth user token so document ACLs are evaluated as the connected user, with silent refresh; 4. falls back to the tenant (bot) token only when the user identity is unrecoverable — the token stayed invalid after a retry, or the refresh itself failed. Identity order is not an optimization: the bot can see strictly less than the user, so the bot is a fallback, never a shortcut. Some endpoints accept only a user access token. Setting requireUserIdentity makes the harness fail with notAuthorized up front instead of retrying as the bot and producing a misleading permission error. Feishu cloud-doc search is the one caller today. URL and token recognition matchRef delegates to parseLarkResourceUrl in lib/twin/ingest/lark-url.ts, which was widened from the twin pipeline's parseLarkDocUrl to cover the two grid kinds. en.title: Provider contract
en.text: DocsProvider, the reference and content shapes, the ten-code error taxonomy, and the registry that refuses duplicate ids and duplicate mention prefixes. Provider contract Everything in this page lives in lib/docs-providers/types.ts and lib/docs-providers/registry.ts. DocsProvider Three properties carry design weight: mentionPrefix is colon-terminated ("lark:") and matches the shape of CHAT NAMESPACE PREFIXES in components/chat/composer-trigger.ts. The registry rejects a prefix that is not. matchRef is pure. The composer calls it on every keystroke, so it must not touch the network or the keyring. It returns everything except providerId and title, both of which the caller fills in. search is optional. A provider without a usable search API omits it; the picker then offers link-pasting, which is a complete answer for a user who already has the link. That is a capability statement, not a failure. Platform is reused from lib/platform/detect.ts ("tauri" "mobile" "web" "headless") rather than a private union, so host gating cannot drift from the app's own detection. Reference and content A RemoteDocRef is cheap: both search and matchRef produce one without fetching a body. format decides the staged attachment's extension and MIME type, which in turn decides how detectDocumentType routes it in lib/chat/attachments/dispatch.ts. wiki stays distinct from doc even though a Feishu wiki node resolves to a document at fetch time: the token namespaces differ (wikcn… vs doxcn…) and the picker labels them differently. Error taxonomy DocsProviderError carries a code and optional params, mirroring LarkIngestError so the Feishu provider can map one onto the other without inventing a second table. Every code has a message under docsProviders.errors. in both locales, so a provider never formats user-facing copy. The picker and the staging toast both look codes up the same way. params is passed straight to the translator, so notAuthorized can name the account and empty can name the document. The reason key is additionally folded into Error.message, which is what appears in logs. Accounts Feishu returns one entry per enabled Lark connector instance — a user may bind several tenants — and the label appends the connected OAuth user's name when there is one. en.title: CUA remote sandbox
en.text: ADR-0020's Dockerized computer-use sandbox: a ghcr.io/trycua/cua-xfce container driven over WebSocket, the lifecycle/registry/protocol/client Rust stack, the Dexie v57 connection registry, and how computer-use actions route local-vs-remote. CUA remote sandbox The CUA sandbox is a remote computer-use target : a ghcr.io/trycua/cua-xfce Docker container runs a computer-server on port 8000; cognia shells docker to launch and probe it, drives it over a WebSocket at /ws, and slots it behind the existing automation gate as a Remote CallTarget. It is fully wired — the container actually launches and computer-use actions route to it. The Tauri commands cua sandbox start / stop / health are registered (lib.rs:693-695); the registry is managed in app state and torn down on exit. Connections are a first-class Dexie entity (schema v57 ). Container lifecycle — lifecycle.rs The container is launched with an ephemeral host port mapped to the container's 8000, then the host port is resolved via docker port. Health is a cheap docker exec true (lifecycle.rs:92-99); docker stop removes the container. Registry — registry.rs CuaSandboxRegistry is a process-scoped map keyed by connection id, holding each container's id, host port, and live WS client. start() is idempotent — a healthy existing container is reused. The registry is created and managed at app start (lib.rs:820-821) and shutdown all() runs on exit (lib.rs:1085-1088), so containers don't leak across sessions. WebSocket protocol — protocol.rs + remote client.rs The computer-server speaks JSON over WS: each message is "command": , "params": . protocol.rs builds these from typed automation actions; a truthy error field signals failure. CuaRemoteClient serializes calls through an mpsc queue — the server processes one command at a time and replies in order, so a spawned pump task sends each request then reads the next text frame as that request's response, with a 30 s call timeout: Target resolution — sandbox-target.ts A computer-use target is either the local host or a remote sandbox referenced by connectionId (never a bare "remote" flag — the id is the convergence anchor). The resolver walks session → character → local: The chat path stamps the resolved id onto the call context: in plugins/computer-use/src/index.ts:73-76, when the target is remote it sets ctx.sandboxConnectionId = target.connectionId, which deserializes in

en.title: Execution sandbox overview
en.text: ADR-0028's five-tier hybrid execution sandbox: the build-options precedence chain that turns it on, how it swaps the SDK builtins for sandbox tools, strict mode, and the audit surface. Execution sandbox overview When a ChatSession has the sandbox enabled, lib/claude/build-options.ts:resolveSendOptions removes the SDK's Bash / Edit / Write builtins and the native text editor, appends a system-prompt note, and stamps the active tier into microvm-bridge. The model is then steered to four sandbox tools (from the cognia-sandboxed-tools plugin) that route to either the OS backend (T1) or the e2b microVM (T4). Tiers T2/T3 cover plugin code; T5 is a per-action policy gate for computer use. There is no bypass — when a backend is unavailable the call denies. The five tiers T1–T5 cover orthogonal threat surfaces. Not every session touches every tier. Tier Protects Mechanism Lives in ------ ------------------------------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------- T1 Bash / Edit / Write / text editor OS-native: bwrap (Linux), sandbox-exec (macOS), runner (Win) OS backends T2 Plugin JS executors Node 24 --permission re-exec from manifest permissions Plugin isolation T3 Plugin WASM modules Wasmtime + WASI, preopens from the grant ledger Plugin isolation T4 Opt-in stronger isolation for T1's tools e2b Firecracker microVM (per-character / per-app tier) microVM & Web T5 computer use (cannot be process-sandboxed) Per-action policy gate (app / window / url / screen-region) Observability & UI What turns it on — the precedence chain The whole feature is gated by one boolean resolved in lib/claude/build-options.ts. The chain walks session → character → app-settings, defaulting to off : The shell tier and the Computer Use target are resolved together into one SandboxSessionBinding (lib/sandbox/binding.ts), each axis walking session → character → app-settings. They are resolved together because choosing the cua-desktop tier means "run shell, files AND GUI in that desktop", so it forces the GUI axis to the same connection. That binding, plus the resolved resource policy and confinement, is then bound once per send into an immutable placement record. resolveSendOptions puts the resulting reference on the send envelope; it is host-only and never reaches a model provider: The per-session set

en.title: Sandbox System
en.text: The four isolation families in cognia-next — the ADR-0028 five-tier execution sandbox, the ADR-0020 CUA remote desktop sandbox, the plugin isolation stack (worker + node --permission + WASM), and the artifact rendering sandbox — and how they relate. Sandbox System "Sandbox" in cognia-next is four distinct families , not one runtime. The big one is the ADR-0028 execution sandbox : a five-tier hybrid (OS-native bwrap / sandbox-exec / Windows runner, Node 24 --permission, Wasmtime, e2b microVM, and a per-action policy gate) that confines Bash / Edit / Write / text editor tool calls. Alongside it sit the CUA remote sandbox (a Dockerized desktop driven over WebSocket — ADR-0020), the plugin isolation stack (renderer PluginSandbox, T2 Node permission re-exec, T3 WASM runtime), and the artifact rendering sandbox (iframe + CSP + DOMPurify — documented in Artifacts / Sandbox). This section maps each module to its source with line-accurate references and the real implementation status (which differs from the ADR proposal in several places). The four families These share the word "sandbox" but are independent subsystems with different threat models and different isolation mechanisms. Read this table first. Family What it isolates Mechanism ADR Status ----------------------- -------------------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---- --------------------------------------- Execution sandbox Model tool calls (Bash / Edit / Write / editor) OS-native (bwrap/sandbox-exec/runner) · microVM · per-action policy 0028 Linux/macOS/Windows real CUA remote sandbox Computer-use (GUI driving) on a remote desktop Docker cua-xfce container driven over WebSocket 0020 Fully wired Plugin isolation Third-party plugin code (JS / Node / WASM) PluginSandbox globals · Node 24 --permission · Wasmtime/WASI 0028 Renderer + T2/T3 wired Rendering sandbox One-shot model artifacts (HTML / SVG / React) iframe + CSP + DOMPurify (see Artifacts / Sandbox) — Stable A fifth, the web code-execution sandbox (lib/sandbox/web), is a deliberate stub today — covered on microVM & Web. en.title: microVM & Web
en.text: The T4 e2b Firecracker microVM tier, the per-session tier router in microvm-bridge, the e2b workspace backend for Marketplace integrations, the web code-execution stub, and the SandboxExecutionResult / consumption-metadata types. microVM & Web lib/sandbox/microvm-bridge.ts is the two-piece glue between the OS sandbox and the e2b microVM tier (T4): a per-session active tier map and a registry holding the microVM exec implementation . The cognia-e2b-sandbox plugin registers a real exec on activate (buildMicrovmExec); the same plugin also provides an E2BWorkspaceBackend for Marketplace integrations. E2B-compatible self-hosted endpoints such as AgentENV can be configured in that plugin's settings via the API URL field. lib/sandbox/web/index.ts is a deliberate stub — the web code-execution runtime is not shipped. types/system/sandbox.ts carries the cross-boundary result and consumption-metadata shapes. The adapter registry — microvm-bridge.ts One registry: the E2B plugin registers and unregisters its exec adapter on activate/deactivate. The per-session "active tier" map this module used to own is gone — the tier now travels on the immutable SandboxRuntimeRef that resolveSendOptions binds (see Execution overview), so it can no longer drift away from the ceiling and the GUI target that were resolved with it. The adapter is owner-scoped : every call names the runtime ref it belongs to, so one E2B workspace can be claimed, reused across a session's calls, and released with the session. The payload shapes mirror the Rust SandboxCommand / PolicyRequest so the OS path and the microVM path are interchangeable from the plugin's point of view. ceiling is the session's resolved cap, carried separately from the per-call request so the adapter can tell "the operator capped this" from "this call simply needs less": The e2b exec adapter — microvm-exec.ts buildMicrovmExec returns a MicrovmExec bound to options. Each call provisions a fresh sandbox, runs the argv joined through bash -c (so quoting matches the OS backend), then closes the sandbox. buildBashCommand (microvm-exec.ts:84-92) exports env vars inline and pipes stdin via AgentENV requires a Linux 6.8+ host with /dev/kvm; 127.0.0.1:8000 works only when Cognia runs on that same host and network namespace. en.text: The Rust execution-sandbox crate: the SandboxedExec trait, the pure policy resolver, the data types, and the real per-platform backends (bwrap / sandbox-exec / Windows runner) with their honest implementation status. OS backends (T1) src-tauri/src/sandbox/ is the Tier-1 OS execution sandbox. The sandbox exec Tauri command derives a SandboxPolicy from the tool name via policy.rs:policy for, selects a per-platform backend via current backend(), and runs the command under that backend. Linux (bwrap), macOS (sandbox-exec), and Windows (cognia-sandbox-runner.exe) are real backends . The Windows runner is the bundled restricted-token + low-integrity + Job Object crate and captures stdout/stderr through its JSON contract. Both Tauri commands are registered (lib.rs:349-350). The trait — traits.rs Every backend implements one async trait. health() is live today (polled by the Settings tab); run() / first time setup() are consumed by the dispatcher. The data model — types.ts types.rs holds the platform-agnostic shapes. A SandboxPolicy is a tagged enum keyed on the tool (Bash / Edit / Write / TextEditor); the network policy is its own tagged enum. en.title: Plugin isolation
en.text: How third-party plugin code is confined: the renderer-side PluginSandbox (permission-mapped globals + Function/AsyncFunction execution), the T2 Node 24 --permission re-exec helper, and the T3 Wasmtime/WASI runtime bounded by the grant ledger. Plugin isolation Three layers confine plugin code. lib/plugin/core/sandbox.ts:PluginSandbox is the shipped renderer-side isolation: it maps each PluginPermission to a concrete allowed global, wraps console / setTimeout / fetch / localStorage, and runs plugin code through a Function / AsyncFunction with explicit args and a timeout. T2 (launchPluginJs.ts) translates a manifest's permissions into Node 24 --permission flags for re-execing Node-target plugins. T3 (wasm-runtime.ts) loads WASM plugins under a runtime whose preopens come from the Dexie grant ledger. T2 is reached through PluginLoader/PluginManager for Node-target frontend plugins, and T3 reconciles manifest preopens before load plus revalidates them before every call. Renderer isolation — PluginSandbox PluginSandbox is constructed with the plugin id, its PluginPermission[], and optional timeout/memory caps. It derives an allow-set and a set of sandboxed globals once, in the constructor. Permission → API mapping A base set of safe globals is always allowed; permissions widen the set: The sandboxed globals are real wrappers, not the raw browser APIs: console — prefixed with [Plugin: ] and routed to the plugin logger (sandbox.ts:137-149). setTimeout — clamped to the configured max (default 30 s) (sandbox.ts:151-158). setInterval — floored at 100 ms to prevent CPU abuse (sandbox.ts:160-167). fetch — stamps an X-Plugin-Id header on every request (sandbox.ts:169-185). localStorage — namespaced to plugin: : with per-key read/write permission checks (sandbox.ts:187-214). Code execution Plugin code runs through a Function (or AsyncFunction) built with explicit argument names so the plugin can only see the globals it was granted — no ambient scope: executeAsync (sandbox.ts:246-273) adds a Promise.race against an "Execution timeout" reject. executeCode(language, code) (sandbox.ts:301-318) requires the sandbox:web-execute permission and delegates to the web sandbox service — which is a stub today (see microVM & Web). en.text: cognia-sandboxed-tools: the in-tree plugin that registers four sandbox MCP tools replacing the SDK's Bash / Edit / Write and the native text editor, and routes each call to the OS sandbox or the e2b microVM. Sandboxed tools plugin plugins/cognia-sandboxed-tools/src/index.ts registers four MCP tools — sandbox bash, sandbox edit, sandbox write, sandbox text editor — that the model uses instead of the SDK builtins when the session has the sandbox enabled. Each call is routed by dispatchSandbox to either the OS sandbox (the sandbox exec Tauri command, T1) or the e2b microVM (T4), based on the active tier for the session. Strict mode: a microvm tier with no registered exec throws — no silent fallback. The four tools The plugin is a frontend plugin that declares tools capability and the native:filesystem / native:process permissions. en.title: Scheduler
en.text: A cross-platform scheduler that promotes tasks from in-app cron to native OS scheduling (Windows Task Scheduler, launchd, systemd). Scheduler Two-layer scheduler — an in-app cron loop for tasks that only matter while Cognia is open, and a native promotion path that mirrors selected tasks to Windows Task Scheduler / launchd / systemd so they fire even when the app is closed. Cognia ships its own scheduler subsystem that runs in two layers: In-app layer — lib/scheduler/ runs cron-defined tasks while the app is open. Native layer — src-tauri/src/scheduler/ promotes tasks to the OS scheduler (Windows Task Scheduler, macOS launchd, Linux systemd) so they fire even when Cognia is closed. Promotion is opt-in per task: lightweight tasks stay in-app; heavy or background-required tasks go native. The full design rationale is in ADR-0002. Where it lives Task model The Trigger and Executor shapes: The full type set lives in lib/scheduler/. Adding a new executor means adding a discriminated-union member and an implementation file under executors/. Cron parser lib/scheduler/cron-parser.ts implements a 5- and 6-field cron parser (with seconds when 6 fields are given). Features: Standard wildcards ( , ,, -, /). Named day-of-week (MON, TUE, …). Named month (JAN, …). Time zone aware via the trigger's timezone field; defaults to system local. The parser produces a next(after: Date) iterator. The scheduling loop calls next() to compute the next fire time, sleeps until then, runs the executor, and repeats. In-app vs native Tasks default to promoted: false. The user can promote a task in the workbench; promotion synthesises: Windows — a Task Scheduler entry pointing at cognia.exe --workspace --task . macOS — a launchd .plist in /Library/LaunchAgents/. Linux — a systemd .timer + .service unit pair under /.config/systemd/user/. metadata store.rs keeps the link between the task UUID and the native task ID (PowerShell task name, plist label, systemd unit name). On task delete, the metadata store also removes the native entry. Tab lock lib/scheduler/tab-lock.ts ensures exactly one tab runs the in-app loop. Implementation: A heartbeat row in Dexie (schedulerLock) updated every 5s. On startup, every tab checks: if the heartbeat is older than 15s, claim the lock; otherwise sleep. If the holder tab closes / crashes, the next tab claims within 15s. This prevents duplicate fires when the us

en.title: Agent Session Import
en.text: Reading other agents' session histories — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Aider, Continue, Gemini CLI — with a two-phase scan that summarizes cheaply and only pays for a full parse on the sessions you actually import. Agent Session Import Stable · ADR-0062 · reuses sessions / messages Nine adapters read the on-disk session histories other agent CLIs leave behind and turn them into Cognia sessions. The design point is the two-phase scan : scan.ts walks the source's roots, reads each matching file exactly once, and produces a SessionSummary through the adapter's lightweight summarizeFile — no full parse, no StoredMessage allocation. The expensive parseSession is paid later and only for the sessions the user actually picks. Import writes into the existing sessions and messages tables, so there is no schema of its own. Design rationale: ADR-0062. Two phases, because a full parse is expensive A user scanning for importable history may be looking at thousands of JSONL files. Parsing all of them to show a picker would be wasteful, so the adapter contract splits in two: Phase Adapter method Cost Produces --- --- --- --- Scan summarizeFile(content, locator) one read per file, no allocation of message objects SessionSummary, or null when the file holds no session Import parseSession full parse the actual messages scan.ts is the shared driver for every per-file JSONL source, so a new adapter only supplies the two methods rather than its own walker. Where it lives Claude Code gets three adapters rather than one because its history is not a flat log: claude-code-dag handles the branching conversation graph and claude-code-subagent the nested subagent transcripts. OpenCode gets two because it ships both a file format and a database. Related

en.title: Authoring and workbench
en.text: Multi-file editing, atomic saves, conflict handling, Codex YAML, and shared Monaco LSP integration. Authoring and workbench Transactional multi-file editor with shared LSP The desktop workbench edits SKILL.md, agents/openai.yaml, and resource files as one logical workspace. Dirty baselines provide content-level conflict detection; Save All commits atomically. Monaco models are mapped to materialized file:// files before standalone LSP document events are sent. Files and save state The file tree always exposes SKILL.md and the virtual agents/openai.yaml, plus every resource at its true relative path. Each open file stores draftContent, savedContent, and one state: clean, saving, saved, blocked, conflict, or error. saveSkillWorkspace compares the current Dexie content with the saved baseline. Metadata-only updatedAt changes do not create a false conflict. Runtime validation or invalid Codex YAML returns blocked; an external content change returns conflict; storage failures return error. Autosave keeps the draft and state so editing or the save shortcut retries it. Save All validates every dirty file first and commits the body, Codex YAML, and resource changes in one transaction. A failure writes nothing and leaves every draft dirty. The “All saved” toast appears only after a real commit. The metadata settings sheet updates metadata only and never submits an unsaved body. Shared LSP workspace lsp-workspace-manager.ts allocates one workspace per Skill, not per tab. It materializes: SKILL.md; agents/openai.yaml when present; every resource under its bundle-relative path. Canvas and Artifact keep single-file synthetic workspaces. Project editors register their real project root and keep real file:// document URIs. The manager maintains bidirectional Monaco URI ↔ materialized URI maps. A Skill model such as skill:///skill-id/scripts/a.ts is sent to the server as its workspace file:// URI; diagnostics, locations, and workspace edits are translated back before Monaco consumes them. Document lifecycle and providers The workbench materializes a document before emitting open. Content changes are ordered, debounced, flushed to disk, then sent as didChange; close emits didClose and workspace teardown removes mappings and files. The registry stores initialize capabilities and registers only declared Monaco providers: completion, hover, definition, references, signature hel

en.title: Built-in skills
en.text: The ADR-0026 typed-tool tier — a code-reviewed registry of MCP tools the assistant calls directly, including desktop plugin conversion and connector operations, gated by PII, access controls, and HITL. Built-in skills ADR-0026 — lib/skills/built-in · typed MCP tools · desktop and connector HITL A built-in skill is a typed MCP tool the model calls , not a prompt snippet. Each one is a frozen BuiltInSkill (types.ts:116) that self-registers at module load (registry.ts:115) and declares a mutation tier (read / write / destructive) plus an imAccess tier. buildBuiltInSkillManifest (manifest.ts:63) projects the registry into MCP tool defs; runBuiltInSkill (dispatcher.ts:58) is the single never-throwing entry point that runs a 6-gate pipeline (registry → Zod → PII → allowlist → IM-access → mutation routing). Write/destructive skills render an A2UI confirm card, persist a skill invoke callback binding (a2ui-mapper.ts:171), and re-enter via the connector bus (bus.ts:893) once the user clicks Confirm. The Lark skills shell out to a user-installed lark-cli (exec-lark-cli.ts:101) with OAuth credentials pulled from the existing Lark connector (auth-bridge.ts:86). Runtime wiring lives in build-options.ts and plugin-tool-ipc.ts. The desktop-only plugin.conversion family instead reuses the deterministic in-app converter and confines all paths to the active workspace. This tier shares the word "built-in" with the five seeded Dexie skill rows (skill builtin concise, skill builtin step by step, …) documented in Data model. Those are prompt snippets appended to the system prompt at send time — the model never "calls" them. The skills on this page are executable typed tools the model invokes via MCP tool-use, with credentials, audit rows, and an HITL round-trip. They live in lib/skills/built-in/, never touch the skills / skillResources Dexie tables, and are filtered in/out per channel by the manifest builder — not by the seeder. en.text: Portable Skill identity, vendor extensions, validation severities, Dexie migration, and transactional persistence. Data model Portable Agent Skills model · Dexie v154 Skill.name is the localized display name. Skill.slug is the stable Agent Skills name and bundle directory. Standard fields, Cognia metadata, unknown frontmatter, and the original Codex YAML are stored separately so import and export can round-trip without conflating display and portable identity. Skill identity and fields packages/agent-config-types/src/index.ts defines the public row. The portability additions are: Field Purpose --- --- slug Lowercase kebab-case portable name, 1–64 characters compatibility Runtime/environment requirements, at most 500 characters metadata Agent Skills string-to-string metadata invocationPolicy implicit or explicit frontmatterExtensions YAML values for fields Cognia does not model codexOpenAiYaml Original agents/openai.yaml text name remains a user-facing display name and may contain non-ASCII text. Existing IDs, character references, status, and native directories are not derived from the slug. Migration Dexie v154 backfills slug without adding an index. Rows are processed in stable createdAt, then id, order. The candidate order is: 1. a valid nativeDirectory basename; 2. a valid existing slug; 3. a normalized display name; 4. skill- plus an ID suffix. Collisions receive -2, -3, and later suffixes while remaining within 64 characters. The migration is idempotent and does not rename external directories. Validation classes lib/skills/validate.ts assigns every issue one severity: runtime: missing body, resource traversal, or duplicate paths; blocks loading or saving. portability: missing description, invalid slug, incompatible directory name, invalid metadata, or length violations; blocks standard bundle export but does not disable a legacy row. warning: compatibility findings that do not block persistence or execution. New rows created in the Skills form must pass runtime and portability validation. Tolerant imports keep legacy data and persist portability findings for repair. Transactional persistence lib/db/skills.ts treats one Skill row and its skillResources as one bundle. en.title: Overview
en.text: The smallest portable capability unit in Cognia — Markdown prompt skills authored in a master-detail workbench, imported from zip/folder/Codex bundles or two marketplaces, mirrored to three on-disk targets, injected as system-prompt suffixes at send time, and complemented by an ADR-0026 tier of 40 typed, HITL-gated built-in tool skills. Skills Subsystem Stable · skills + skillResources tables since Dexie v8 (DB v72) · ADR-0026 built-in tier at schema v43 A Skill is a SKILL.md-shaped row — name, Markdown body, optional allowedTools, plus bundled scripts/ / references/ / assets/ resources. The browser source of truth is Dexie (lib/db/skills.ts); everything else is a pipeline in or out of that table: a bundle importer (lib/skills/bundle/loader.ts:65) for zip / folder / OpenAI-Codex layouts, a two-source marketplace (skills-lock.json registry + the skills.sh directory), a three-target native sync (lib/skills/sync.ts:145 → skills install mirrored writing cognia / /.claude/skills / /.agents/skills), and the send-time injector (lib/claude/build-options.ts:378) that appends enabled skills to the system prompt and unions their allowedTools. A separate ADR-0026 tier — lib/skills/built-in/ — exposes 40 typed Lark skills as agent tools with PII, allowlist, and HITL gates; those never touch the Dexie table. Two very different things both answer to the name "skill" in this codebase, and this section keeps them strictly apart: 1. Prompt skills — Dexie rows whose Markdown body is appended to the system prompt at send time. Authored in the workbench, imported, synced, sold on the marketplace. They are never executed . 2. Built-in tool skills — code-reviewed TypeScript modules (lib/skills/built-in/) registered as MCP-shaped tools the model calls , wrapping lark-cli with a six-gate dispatcher. ADR-0026. The original design rationale lives in ADR-0026 for the built-in tier; the prompt-skill side grew organically and is documented here module by module, against the current implementation. en.title: Loading and injection
en.text: Desktop hybrid progressive disclosure, scoped loader tools, resources, tool policy, and usage accounting. Loading and injection Hybrid progressive loading on desktop chat Skills attached for the current message are injected in full. Character and surface Skills are advertised as a compact catalog and loaded on demand through session-scoped, read-only tools. Explicit-only Skills never enter the implicit catalog. Effective set resolveSendOptions first resolves enabled Skills from character references and ephemeral message attachments. Session-disabled rows are removed. invocationPolicy: explicit removes a character Skill from implicit discovery; the same Skill remains usable when the user attaches it explicitly. The effective allowedTools set is the union from only: explicitly attached Skills; and Skills present in the implicit catalog. disallowedTools is applied later and always wins. Hybrid prompt Explicit attachments include the full body, a resource manifest, and UTF-8 resources marked inline. Implicit Skills contribute only ID, slug, display name, and description. The catalog instructs the model to call load skill before following an unloaded Skill. Catalog-authored built-ins may declare metadata.default-enabled: true. Seeding applies that default only when the row is first created and preserves a later user disable. Diagram Design uses this path: it is discoverable for drawing intent without injecting its full body or its 27 type references into ordinary turns. Inline resource text across one Skill is capped at 64 KiB. Files beyond the cap remain in the manifest for on-demand reads. Scoped loader tools Every send creates an in-memory context keyed by session. It contains only Skills available in that turn. The context is replaced on the next send and released when the turn completes. load skill returns the body, resource manifest, inline text, and a hint when non-inline text exists. load skill resource accepts skill id, a normalized relative path, and optional byte offset and limit. A page is at most 64 KiB and never splits a UTF-8 code point. Binary resources return MIME type and size only; base64 content is never dumped into model context. Guessing another Skill ID, traversing a path, or reading a resource owned by another Skill is rejected. en.title: Native sync & security
en.text: Bidirectional sync between the Dexie skill store and on-disk /.claude / Codex / cognia mirrors — the push/pull pipeline with fingerprint precheck and conflict resolution, the Rust install layer (multi-target mirrors, symlink-or-copy, trash), the 13-command IPC surface, and the advisory regex security scanner. Native sync & security Desktop only — lib/skills/sync.ts · src-tauri/src/skills (7 files, 13 commands) The Dexie skill store is the source of truth; the on-disk SKILL.md tree is what other Claude tooling actually reads. lib/skills/sync.ts pushes rows out and pulls disk edits back in, matching by nativeDirectory then name slug (sync.ts:260-262) and gating every direction with a SHA-256 fingerprint (sync.ts:58-86). The Rust side (src-tauri/src/skills/) writes the canonical copy under /cognia/skills/ and projects it to /.claude/skills/ + /.agents/skills/ as symlinks on Unix, copies on Windows (install.rs:226-304), moving prior copies to .trash/ on fingerprint change. A 13-command IPC surface (lib/claude/ipc.ts:381-440, registered lib.rs:398-410) covers scan, install, trash, remote-fetch, registry, and an advisory-only 9-rule regex security scanner (scanner.rs:59-126). Everything no-ops in the browser — isTauri() guards return an (env) error (sync.ts:147-148). Why two copies exist Cognia stores skills as IndexedDB rows (see data model), but Claude Code, the Codex CLI, and Cognia's own sidecar all read skills from disk as /.claude/skills/ /SKILL.md. Native sync reconciles the two views so a skill authored in the app is discoverable verbatim by those CLIs, and a skill an external CLI wrote is importable back into Dexie without a manual conversion step (native.rs:1-5). en.title: Source Control
en.text: A VS Code-shaped Git panel over a native Rust backend — 65 Tauri commands with a 1:1 TypeScript surface, a filesystem watcher, interactive rebase and the sequencer, plus AI commit messages, diff explanations and review. Source Control Stable · ADR-0038 Git is implemented in Rust (crates/cognia-git/), not shelled out from the renderer, and exposed as 65 Tauri commands with an almost exactly matching TypeScript surface of 67 functions in lib/git/commands.ts — a rare 1:1 backend/frontend mapping with no dormant half. The panel (51 components under components/source-control/) is VS Code-shaped: staging by hunk, a commit graph, blame, stash, worktrees and interactive rebase driven through sequencer.rs. Three AI helpers sit on top — commit-message generation, diff explanation and review — each built as prompt builders plus one generate call, so the prompt construction is testable without a model. Design rationale: ADR-0038. Panel preferences live in AppSettings.gitSettings.panel — this subsystem has no Dexie tables of its own. The Rust layer is the whole of Git Each file in crates/cognia-git/src/ owns one area of Git, which is what keeps the command surface flat rather than a single god-object: watcher.rs is why the panel does not poll: the backend watches the repository and pushes change events, consumed on the TS side through lib/git/events.ts. Frontend modules The AI helpers are prompt builders first Each helper splits into pure prompt construction plus a single generate call, so the interesting part is unit-testable without a model in the loop. ai-commit.ts exposes buildCommitSystemPrompt(), buildCommitUserPrompt(), clampDiff() — which trims a diff to a character budget before it reaches the model — and stripFences(), with generateCommitMessage() (lib/git/ai-commit.ts:102) as the only model-touching function. ai-explain.ts follows the same shape with generateDiffExplanation(). en.title: Overview
en.text: ADR-0090's unified agent execution authority — one resolver freezes runtime, route, host and credentials into an immutable spec; the sidecar dispatches on it; the gateway routes it with tickets; every caller (chat, workflow, team, plugin) funnels through one service. Unified Agent Execution ADR-0090 · flag-gated rollout (agentExecutionResolverV2) · spec version 1 Cognia has exactly three agent runtime rails — the Claude Agent SDK, the provider-neutral AI SDK loop (both hosted by the Node sidecar), and external agents behind the ExternalAgentManager. Everything else is a dimension , not a rail: gateway vs direct is a route , desktop vs headless is a host , native vs orchestrated is a delegation mode , and the text-only executeAgent channel is a completion fallback , never a fourth runtime. The authority chain Once a spec exists for a session, nobody re-derives runtime, route, host or credentials from anything else. The spec's executionFingerprint (canonical-JSON FNV-1a-128, volatile fields excluded) is the identity that tickets, budgets, recovery and audits key on. Fail-closed rules A hard capability (policy.requires) the frozen runtime cannot serve rejects before any provider call — a completion is never silently consumed instead (AgentCapabilityUnsatisfiedError). Losing the agent host degrades to the completion rail only when the policy explicitly allows it (fallbackPolicy: "completion"), and the result then carries a machine-readable degradedReason that surfaces on workflow node outputs, team dispatch results, and plugin meta. Headless/managed installs prohibit the legacy completion fallback outright. Wire shape The spec rides SendOptions.execution (AgentExecutionSendSpec) — secret free by construction: gateway routes carry an endpoint plus a ticket id ; direct routes carry a credential profile reference . Raw keys stay on the existing sendOptions.env redaction path. The Rust SendOptions flattens unknown fields, so the sidecar receives the spec unchanged and its dispatch (sidecar/dispatch/index.mjs) routes on execution.runtimeAdapter, counting spec-less sends as legacy dispatch telemetry. Requests on a ticket bypass alias/decide entirely; unmapped models 400; credential resolution happens per attempt at send time; failover is pre-first-byte only, sticky affinity never switches accounts on 401/403. Snapshot publication is CAS'd (profileVersion + authority) — no last-writer-wins between desktop and headless publishers. Probes and opt-ins are typed out of the gate: they cannot reach certifiedPath because only evaluateCompatibilityGate output can construct it. en.text: Heterogeneous teammate execution bindings, delegation depth, the run budget governor, canonical sessions with honest fidelity, and strict-dominance recovery. Teams, Delegation and Recovery Execution bindings (Phase 7) A teammate binds inherit pinned pool (TeammateConfig.execution), resolved by fixed precedence managed member run team default app default — the managed override is explicit in the decision trace. Pool mode exposes candidate deployment ids only (first candidate is today's deterministic pick). New raw apiKey/baseURL teammate writes are rejected at every store path; legacy rows stay readable and migrate to their provider-id deployment ref at dispatch. decideDelegationMode classifies native vs orchestrated on six axes (runtime, route, host, deployment, credential, hard capabilities): only frozen model-role variance stays native. Provider- or external-pinned subagent defs are excluded from the SDK-native agents map — the orchestrated dispatch agent rail honors them instead of the SDK silently mis-running them. Team-to-team delegation carries a validated secret-free HandoffEnvelope and a maxTeamDelegationDepth gate (default 2). One RunBudgetGovernor ledgers every child's usage, attempts and failures on the root pool; the plugin budget rebases on it. en.title: Unified Subscription
en.text: One account model across Anthropic, Codex and OpenCode — keyring-backed provider vaults, an ordered limits-source registry that prefers a real utilization window over a credit meter, nine balance adapters, and an encrypted export envelope. Unified Subscription Stable · ADR-0025 · keyring v2 / v20 Three subscription providers — Anthropic, Codex, OpenCode — share one account model, one vault format and one limits surface. The interesting piece is the limits-source registry (lib/subscription/limits/registry.ts): a flat ordered list where windowed sources come before the generic balance source, so the runner prefers a real utilization window and only falls through to a credit meter when no window applies. Aggregation (limits/aggregate.ts) queries every configured account and returns them with the active one pinned first — which is what both the TUI /limits panel and the desktop multi-provider view consume. Every seam is injected, so the same code runs offline in tests and in the CLI with a Node-fetch-backed authedGet. Design rationale: ADR-0025. Codex-specific expansion is in ADR-0048. Order is the design A "limit" can mean two different things: a rolling utilization window (Anthropic, Codex) or a credit balance (most OpenAI-compatible resellers). Presenting a credit meter when a real window exists would be a downgrade, so the registry encodes the preference as list order — windowed sources first, the generic balance source last. The runner walks the returned candidate list and stops at the first source that yields a snapshot. Plugin-contributed sources overlay in front of the built-ins, resolved through lib/plugin/registries/limits-source-registry.ts. The registry itself is pure: a list plus a resolver that returns every matching source rather than picking one, which keeps the fallback decision in the runner where it can be tested. en.text: n8n-style visual orchestration layer — wire characters, teams, skills, twins, connectors, and AI primitives into executable graphs with durable run history, a hybrid Rust/TS runtime, and an AI co-pilot. Visual Workflows A React Flow v12 editor (Zustand + zundo store, elkjs auto-layout) over 153 node kinds in 7 categories , executed by a hybrid runtime : Rust owns when a workflow starts (cron daemon, HMAC webhook receiver) and whether a run survived a crash (SQLite mirror); TS owns how a run walks the graph step by step (runWorkflow — validate → topo-sort → step loop → durable event log). The graph type is VisualWorkflow (types/workflow/visual.ts:242, schemaVersion: 1); workflow persistence spans 13 Dexie tables through schema v156. An AI co-pilot drafts Zod-validated batch proposals the user previews and applies as a single undo step. cognia-next uses this layer to compose its mature runtime entities — characters, agent teams, skills, employee twins, platform connectors, MCP servers, and plugins — into executable graphs. The design follows ADR 0011 (subsystem), ADR 0017 (plugin extension points), and ADR 0034 (editor completeness). The one load-bearing principle Rust owns "when does the workflow start" and "did this run survive the crash". TS owns "given a run, how do we walk through the steps one by one". Everything else falls out of that split. Cron firing and webhook receipt must work while the webview is minimized to the tray, so they live in Rust (src-tauri/src/workflow/). The step-by-step orchestration touches Dexie, the LLM clients, the connector bus, and the agent-team runtime — all of which live in the webview — so it stays in TS (lib/workflow/runtime/). The two sides communicate through Tauri events plus scoped trigger, run-mirror, and durable-waitpoint IPC commands. en.title: Runtime execution engine
en.text: The TypeScript runtime in lib/workflow/runtime that topo-sorts a VisualWorkflow, schedules steps with bounded in-run concurrency, retries with exponential backoff, persists an idempotent event log, and recovers crashed runs by replay. Runtime execution engine lib/workflow/runtime/orchestrator.ts:118 runWorkflow(input) is the core: it validates, persists a WorkflowRunRow (orchestrator.ts:142), wires a single run-level AbortController plus wall-clock timeout (orchestrator.ts:165-203), topo-sorts the VisualWorkflow (topo-sort.ts:23), then runs a ready-set scheduler loop (orchestrator.ts:443-471) that respects an in-run maxConcurrency budget. Each step goes through step-executor.ts:56 runStep with cache short-circuit, resolveDeep param resolution, a retry-with-backoff loop (step-executor.ts:142-160, attempts 3 / exponential / baseMs 1000 / maxMs 30000, no jitter), and per-step timeout (step-executor.ts:186). Every transition is appended to workflowRunEvents via event-log.ts:21, and IdempotencyCache.hydrate(runId) (idempotency.ts:33) replays only the completed steps of that run, so crash recovery (resume-controller.ts:29) re-runs the same runId and skips finished work. A few wrappers that need richer unions bypass withPlugin and call the loader directly in try/catch: camera.pickPhoto (:85), geolocation.getCurrentPosition (:70), barcode.scan (:53), biometric.verify (:88), share.share (:45). en.title: Discovery & Pairing
en.text: How a phone finds and trusts a desktop — mDNS subscribe, the LAN IP-range scanner, the WebRTC-ICE local-IP trick, the prioritized connection-strategy candidate walk, the three-step pairing wizard, the QR payload, and TLS fingerprint pinning. Discovery & Pairing Before a phone can call anything it must (a) find a desktop and (b) establish trust. Discovery is two distinct systems: lan-scanner.ts discovers unknown hosts (parallel mDNS subscribe + IP-range probe, accepting a 401 from /api/whoami as proof-of-Cognia), while connection-strategy.ts resolves a known paired device's reachable URL by walking a prioritized candidate list (mDNS → tunnel → cached) and probing /healthz. Trust is the canonical pairing wizard: scan or paste a cgnp3 payload, validate Host/tenant/expiry/version, register independent P-256 device and signaling keys with an Owner invitation or OIDC session, and atomically persist the resulting public target plus encrypted private keys. The local IP needed for scanning is recovered via a WebRTC ICE trick (local-ip.ts:50) because mobile WebViews can't read network interfaces. Two discovery systems They share the fingerprint-pinning idea but no code — keep them distinct: lan-scanner.ts — discover unknown hosts. Used by the pairing wizard's Discover step to surface desktops the phone has never seen. connection-strategy.ts — reach a known host. Used at call time to pick the best URL for an already-paired device whose fingerprint is known. LAN scanner — scanLan (lan-scanner.ts:131) Runs an mDNS subscribe (:177) and an IP-range probe in parallel, racing against a 5-second mDNS window or abort (:225): A candidate is accepted only if it returns HTTP 401 with a code,message body (evaluateProbeResponse, :409-432) — an unauthenticated request to /api/whoami should be rejected, which is exactly what proves the host is a Cognia server. The result is then enriched with the TLS fingerprint via healthz. Default port 27890 (:110); the extra ports [27890, 7890, 7891, 7900, 8443] (:119) are tried only for paired/emulator IPs. The local-IP trick — local-ip.ts:50 A mobile WebView can't enumerate network interfaces, so getPrivateLocalIps() opens a STUN-less RTCPeerConnection with a dummy data channel and harvests the host ICE candidates (:50), filtering to RFC-1918 ranges (isPrivateIpv4, :151). enumerateSlash24() (:159) then expands a discovered IP to its /24 for the

en.title: Mobile Architecture
en.text: The mobile companion — one Next.js static export wrapped by Capacitor 8, connected to a Host over target-aware Tauri IPC / HTTPS+WS / WebRTC, with native bridges, cgnp3 + DPoP pairing, secure storage, and offline-first Dexie sync. Mobile Architecture beta · V2 + WebRTC Cognia's mobile client is not a separate React Native app and not a trimmed desktop build — it is the same out/ static export wrapped by Capacitor 8 inside an iOS/Android WebView, then connected back to the desktop's External API. One JS bundle, three shells (Tauri / Capacitor / Web), one shared React codebase. The seam is the Transport interface: desktop uses TauriTransport, while Web/Capacitor bind CompanionTransport whenever the account's active runtime target is a paired Host. Each transport.call(name, args) resolves to Tauri IPC, an HTTPS DPoP rpc POST, or an upgraded WebRTC DataChannel. Native capabilities go through lib/capacitor/ wrappers that degrade to unsupported off-device, and reads come from a local Dexie that syncs incrementally. The thesis: one bundle, three shells mobile/capacitor.config.ts sets webDir: "../out" (:17); src-tauri/tauri.conf.json sets frontendDist: "../out". Both native shells point at the same directory a single pnpm build produces. The React running inside the iOS/Android WebView is byte-for-byte the React that runs in Tauri — same Zustand stores, same Dexie schema, same useTranslations() calls. Only two things differ at runtime: which Transport the selector returns, and which enum usePlatform() reports. Option Verdict --- --- Tauri 2 Mobile Rejected — mobile lacks sidecar support; the Claude Agent SDK sidecar is a core desktop runtime. React Native Rejected — rewriting 57 shadcn/ui components to RN primitives for zero functional gain. Capacitor 8 Adopted — drop the existing static export into a native WebView, no UI rewrite. The deeper truth: the phone is never a sidecar runtime. The Claude Agent SDK needs Node ≥ 20 and native extensions; connector webhooks can't expose a public URL from behind carrier NAT. So five subsystems are "desktop-only" by platform reality — the desktop is the true server, the phone a trusted client. See ADR-0014. The client spine A mobile session walks a fixed spine: discover the desktop, pair with it, choose a transport , sync local data, and reach native capabilities. en.title: Sync & Offline
en.text: The runSyncDown orchestrator, the 10 per-table sync handlers, paginated deltas with a monotonic cursor, the durable cursor store, the allowlist-merge for settings, the four sync triggers, and the Dexie-first query hook. Sync & Offline beta · offline-first The phone keeps its own Dexie database and reads from it first; the network only fills it in. The engine is runSyncDown (companion-sync.ts:161), which iterates 10 registered table handlers in order, each calling the sync pull RPC with its last cursor and applying the returned delta (bulkPut + tombstone bulkDelete) through the generic runSyncHandler (base.ts:52). Cursors persist per-table in Dexie (cursor-store.ts) and advance only monotonically. Four triggers drive a sync — foreground, event-driven, network-up, and resume — and useDexieFirstQuery (use-dexie-first-query.ts:54) is the read primitive that renders from Dexie immediately and kicks a background sync on mount. The orchestrator runSyncDown(opts) (companion-sync.ts:161) iterates DEFAULT HANDLERS (:52, the 10 tables in execution order) sequentially (:174). A re-entrancy gate (inflight, :163) prevents overlap except for targeted opts.only runs. For each handler it reads the table's cursor (:176), calls run(t, since ) (:177), applies a monotonic guard (nextSince since, :186) so a stale response can't rewind the cursor, and fire-and-forget-persists the new cursor (:196). ensureHydrated() (:98) loads the cursor map once on first run. The handlers Each handler is thin — it delegates to runSyncHandler (base.ts:52), which drains pages until !has more (cap MAX PAGES = 100, :38), bulkPuts rows and bulkDeletes tombstones keyed by id: Handler Table Strategy Entry --- --- --- --- syncCharacters characters bulkPut; filters built-ins characters.ts:15 syncSkills skills bulkPut skills.ts:8 syncSessions sessions bulkPut sessions.ts:8 syncMessages messages bulkPut, paged messages.ts:14 syncWorkflows workflows bulkPut; filters built-ins workflows.ts:14 syncTwinProfile twinProfile bulkPut twin-profile.ts:13 syncPlugins plugins bulkPut plugins.ts:12 syncAdapterInstances adapterInstances bulkPut adapter-instances.ts:13 syncConversationOverrides conversationOverrides bulkPut conversation-overrides.ts:14 syncAppSettings settings allowlist-merge app-settings.ts:66 These mirror the server's sync-table allowlist one-for-one. en.title: Transport Layer
en.text: The Transport interface, the tri-state selector, CompanionTransport (HTTPS rpc + WSS events with replay), the WebRTC sub-tier, the TLS-pinned fetch, the four transport tiers, and the SecureStorage credential store. Transport Layer Transport (transport-types.ts:19) is a two-method interface — call(name, args) and subscribe(event, handler) — that every part of the shared bundle uses instead of touching Tauri or HTTP directly. Desktop binds TauriTransport; web and Capacitor rebind to CompanionTransport when the account's active runtime target is a paired Host, otherwise web stays on its standalone target. CompanionTransport (transport-companion.ts) POSTs to /api/ rpc/ with a five-minute P-256 DPoP-bound access token and opens /ws/events with a single-use socket ticket plus ?since= replay. It transparently upgrades to a WebRTC DataChannel sub-tier (transport-rtc.ts) and falls back to HTTPS/WS on failure. Private keys live only in OS secure storage or the Browser Vault. The interface lib/tauri.ts is the public barrel — it re-exports the singleton transport, the isTauri / isCapacitor detectors, and the plugin wrappers. Nothing in app/, components/, or hooks/ constructs a transport; they import transport and call it. Runtime-target selection RuntimeTargetRegistry keeps targets account-scoped and gives every target a separate Dexie database. Activation stops old subscriptions, switches the database, rebinds the transport, then refreshes the manifest and sync cursor; failure rolls back the active pointer. WebRTC remains a sub-tier inside CompanionTransport, not a separate application transport.
